docs.title: C++ Course for Competitive Programming
docs.text: This course is designed to teach C++ from the ground up, with a focus on competitive programming, contests, and algorithmic problem solving.

docs.title: Algorithmic Complexity
docs.text:
Every competitive programming problem is a negotiation between what you want to compute and what the judge will let you compute. Complexity analysis is the tool that makes that negotiation explicit: it tells you, before you write a single line of code, whether your planned algorithm will fit in the time and memory limit. A contestant who can look at n ≤ 10^5 and immediately think "$O(n \log n)$ required, $O(n)$ ideal, $O(n \sqrt{n})$ borderline, $O(n^2)$ impossible" has already solved half the problem — they know which algorithmic family to reach for. A contestant who cannot will spend thirty minutes coding an $O(n^2)$ DP that TLEs on test 5.

This article covers the notation, the calculation rules, the STL-specific constants that Big-O hides, and — most importantly — the practical mapping between constraints and complexities that judges actually enforce.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Introduction to C++ — -O2, the CP template.
  • I/O and Data Types — int vs long long, the overflow traps.
  • Conditionals and Loops — loop idioms, off-by-one.
  • Arrays and Vectors — contiguous memory, cache behavior.
  • Functions and Recursion — stack frames, recursion depth.
  • STL Basics — containers and their asymptotic costs.

docs.title: What Complexity Measures
docs.text:
Algorithmic complexity measures how the resource consumption of an algorithm scales with input size $n$. Two resources matter in CP:

  • Time complexity — the number of elementary operations (roughly: CPU instructions) as a function of $n$.
  • Space complexity — the amount of auxiliary memory (heap, stack, arrays) as a function of $n$, excluding the input in most contest conventions.

Why "scaling" and not "exact count"? Because exact counts depend on the machine, the compiler, the optimizer, and dozens of microarchitectural details. Two implementations of the same algorithm can differ by 10× in wall-clock time and still be "the same complexity". What is invariant across machines is the growth rate: doubling $n$ roughly quadruples the operations of an $O(n^2)$ algorithm, regardless of whether those operations take 1 ns or 10 ns.

The judge cares about absolute time (typically 1–2 seconds), but you can only reason about relative growth. The bridge between them is the empirical fact that on modern judges, an $O(n)$ algorithm with a simple body does roughly $10^8$–$10^9$ operations per second. This constant is stable enough across judges to be a design tool (more on this in the benchmarks section).

docs.title: Asymptotic Notation — Big-O, Big-Omega, Big-Theta
docs.text:
Most CP tutorials only teach Big-O. That is enough for choosing algorithms, but not for understanding why some comparisons are subtler than they look. Here is the full picture, briefly.

Notation Meaning Analogy $O(f(n))$ Upper bound: $T(n) \le c \cdot f(n)$ for large $n$ "$T$ grows no faster than $f$" $\Omega(f(n))$ Lower bound: $T(n) \ge c \cdot f(n)$ for large $n$ "$T$ grows at least as fast as $f$" $\Theta(f(n))$ Tight bound: both $O(f)$ and $\Omega(f)$ "$T$ grows exactly like $f$"

In competitive programming, when someone says "this algorithm is $O(n \log n)$", they almost always mean $\Theta(n \log n)$ — the tight bound. Big-O is used as shorthand for "the dominant term". The distinction matters in a few places:

  • Saying "bubble sort is $O(n^2)$" is true but uninformative — it's also $O(n^3)$, $O(2^n)$, and $O(n!)$, because Big-O is only an upper bound. The tight statement is $\Theta(n^2)$.
  • Saying "unordered_map lookup is $O(1)$" is misleading — the worst case is $O(n)$ when every key collides. The honest statement is average $O(1)$, worst $O(n)$. This matters enormously in CP (see the anti-hash section).
  • Saying "vector::push_back is $O(1)$" is imprecise — the honest statement is amortized $O(1)$: a single push_back can cost $O(n)$ when reallocation occurs, but the average over $n$ pushes is $O(1)$.

For design purposes, assume everyone means the tightest bound unless stated otherwise, and always ask "worst case or average?" when the answer involves hashing.

docs.title: Common Time Complexities
docs.text:
Listed in increasing order of growth. The rightmost columns tell you when each is viable under a 1–2 second limit.

Complexity Name Typical $n$ limit Common example $O(1)$ constant any $n$ array index, unordered_map avg lookup, bitset count $O(\log n)$ logarithmic up to $10^{18}$ (integer math) binary search, set::find, bit length $O(\sqrt{n})$ square root $10^{12}$–$10^{14}$ trial division, sqrt decomposition, block algorithms $O(n)$ linear $10^7$–$10^8$ array scan, prefix sum, BFS/DFS $O(n \log n)$ linearithmic $10^5$–$10^6$ merge sort, std::sort, FFT, sieve of Eratosthenes $O(n \sqrt{n})$ — $10^4$–$10^5$ Mo's algorithm, sqrt-decomposition on arrays $O(n^2)$ quadratic $10^3$–$10^4$ double loop, Floyd–Warshall on dense, naive DP $O(n^2 \log n)$ — $10^3$ Fenwick tree 2D on medium $n$ $O(n^3)$ cubic $10^2$–$500$ Floyd–Warshall, matrix multiplication (naive), triple DP $O(2^n)$ exponential $n \le 20$ (subset enumeration) brute-force subsets, naive TSP $O(n \cdot 2^n)$ — $n \le 18$ bitmask DP $O(n!)$ factorial $n \le 10$–$12$ brute-force permutations, naive TSP

The $n$ limits are approximations for simple operations under -O2 in 1–2 seconds. The actual threshold depends on the operation's constant factor — see the benchmarks section below.

docs.title: Rule 1 — Sequential adds, nested multiplies
docs.text:
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { /* O(1) */ }        // O(n)
sort(v.begin(), v.end());                          // O(n log n)
// Total: O(n) + O(n log n) = O(n log n) — dominated by the larger term

for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)                        // n iterations
    for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j) { /* O(1) */ }    // × m iterations
// Total: O(n · m)

The dominant term wins. O(n^2 + n log n + n) = O(n^2). Lower-order terms are always dropped.

docs.title: Rule 2 — Loops halved or doubled → logarithmic
docs.text:
If the loop variable is divided or multiplied by a constant, the loop runs $O(\log n)$ times:

for (int i = n; i > 0; i /= 2) { /* O(1) */ }     // log_2(n) iterations
for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 3) { /* O(1) */ }     // log_3(n) iterations

The base of the logarithm does not matter for complexity (it's a constant factor), so both are $O(\log n)$. In practice, base 2 is what you get from binary search, and $n = 10^{18}$ requires only 60 iterations.

docs.title: Rule 3 — Loops with non-trivial step sizes
docs.text:
The outer loop runs $O(n)$ times but the inner loop runs fewer times depending on the outer index — a harmonic series:

for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
    for (int j = 1; j <= n / i; ++j) { /* O(1) */ }
// Inner total: n/1 + n/2 + n/3 + ... + n/n = n · H(n) ≈ n · ln(n) = O(n log n)

This pattern appears in sieve-like algorithms and divisor enumeration. Recognizing it as $O(n \log n)$ (not $O(n^2)$) is a common step in optimizing number-theoretic code.

Another common pattern — two pointers on a sorted array:

int j = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    while (j < n && a[i] + a[j] < target) ++j;
    // ...
}
// Although it looks like O(n^2) (nested loops), j only advances: total O(n)

The key observation: j never goes backwards, so the inner while runs at most $n$ times in total across the entire outer loop. Amortized analysis over both loops gives $O(n)$, not $O(n^2)$.

docs.title: Rule 4 — Recursion via recurrence relations
docs.text:
For a recursive algorithm, write the recurrence $T(n)$ = (work per call) + (sum of recursive call costs). Three common patterns:

A. Halving with constant work → $O(\log n)$

Binary search: $T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)$. Solved by unrolling: $T(n) = O(1) \cdot \log_2(n) = O(\log n)$.

int binary_search(int lo, int hi, int target) {
    if (lo > hi) return -1;
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
    if (a[mid] < target) return binary_search(mid + 1, hi, target);
    return binary_search(lo, mid - 1, target);
}
// T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n)

B. Two halving calls with linear work → $O(n \log n)$

Merge sort: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$. The Master Theorem (case 2) gives $O(n \log n)$.

void merge_sort(int l, int r) {
    if (l >= r) return;
    int mid = (l + r) / 2;
    merge_sort(l, mid);
    merge_sort(mid + 1, r);
    merge(l, mid, r);        // O(r - l) = O(n)
}
// T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n log n)

C. Two calls with overlapping subproblems → exponential

Naive Fibonacci: $T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1)$. The recursion tree has as many leaves as Fibonacci numbers, so $T(n) = \Theta(\phi^n)$ where $\phi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2 \approx 1.618$. The common upper bound $O(2^n)$ is not tight — the true growth is base $\phi$, not base 2. Both bounds are exponential, but the difference matters numerically: at $n = 40$, $\phi^{40} \approx 2.3 \cdot 10^8$ while $2^{40} \approx 10^{12}$ — a factor of ~4000. The honest statement is $\Theta(\phi^n)$, and the practical implication is that naive Fibonacci is already impractical at $n = 40$, not $n = 60$ as $O(2^n)$ might suggest.

long long fib(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);   // T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) = Θ(φ^n)
}

The Master Theorem handles recurrences of the form $T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n)$:

Case Condition Result 1 $f(n) = O(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon > 0$ $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a})$ 2 $f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a})$ $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log n)$ 3 $f(n) = \Omega(n^{\log_b a + \epsilon})$ and regularity holds $T(n) = \Theta(f(n))$

For merge sort: $a = 2, b = 2, f(n) = n$. $\log_2 2 = 1$, $f(n) = \Theta(n^1)$ — case 2, so $T(n) = \Theta(n \log n)$.

For binary search: $a = 1, b = 2, f(n) = 1$. $\log_2 1 = 0$, $f(n) = \Theta(n^0)$ — case 2, so $T(n) = \Theta(\log n)$.

For naive matrix multiplication by divide-and-conquer: $a = 8, b = 2, f(n) = n^2$. $\log_2 8 = 3$, $f(n) = O(n^{3 - \epsilon})$ — case 1, so $T(n) = \Theta(n^3)$. (Strassen's algorithm reduces $a$ to 7 and gets $O(n^{\log_2 7}) \approx O(n^{2.807})$.)

Master Theorem does not handle all recurrences — it misses $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n \log n)$, for instance. But it covers the vast majority of divide-and-conquer algorithms you will encounter.

docs.title: Rule 5 — Memory and stack
docs.text:
Space complexity follows the same rules, applied to allocations and stack depth:

// O(1) auxiliary space
long long sum(const vector<int>& v) {
    long long s = 0;
    for (int x : v) s += x;
    return s;
}

// O(n) auxiliary space — the copy is the whole point
vector<int> double_all(const vector<int>& v) {
    vector<int> out(v.size());
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)v.size(); ++i) out[i] = 2 * v[i];
    return out;
}

// O(h) stack space where h = tree depth
void dfs(int u) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj[u]) if (!visited[v]) dfs(v);
}
// For a balanced tree: h = O(log n). For a skewed (path) tree: h = O(n).

The recursion stack space is part of the total space complexity, and it is the source of the "recursion works fine on small trees but crashes on 10^5-node paths" pattern from the previous article. A $10^5$-node recursion with a ~64-byte frame uses ~6 MB of stack, already near the typical 8 MB limit.

docs.title: Amortized Analysis
docs.text:
Some operations are individually expensive but cheap on average across a sequence of operations. The canonical example is vector::push_back:

vector<int> v;
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) v.push_back(i);

push_back is $O(1)$ most of the time, but when the vector is full, it allocates a new buffer of 2× the current capacity, copies all existing elements, and frees the old buffer — an $O(n)$ operation at that moment. Without amortization, one might fear the total is $O(n^2)$ for $n$ pushes. It is not.

The argument. Let the capacities at each reallocation be $1, 2, 4, 8, \dots, 2^k$ where $2^k \le n < 2^{k+1}$. The reallocation at size $2^i$ copies $2^i$ elements. Total copying:

$$ \sum_{i=0}^{k} 2^i = 2^{k+1} - 1 < 2n = O(n) $$

So the total work over $n$ push_backs is $O(n)$, giving an amortized cost of $O(1)$ per operation. The geometric growth factor (2×) is what makes this work. A growth factor of 1.1× (like std::string in some implementations) would also give amortized $O(1)$, but with a larger constant.

Amortized analysis is not average-case analysis. Average-case refers to random inputs; amortized refers to a guaranteed worst-case bound across a sequence of operations, with no randomness. push_back is amortized $O(1)$ even on adversarial sequences — there is no input that makes $n$ push_backs take worse than $O(n)$ total.

The same argument applies to:

  • unordered_map insertion (rehashing at 2× growth).
  • deque::push_front and deque::push_back.
  • priority_queue::push and pop (sift up/down).
  • Union-find with path compression: $O(\alpha(n))$ amortized per operation, where $\alpha$ is the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant for any $n$ you will encounter.

Amortization does not apply to:

  • vector::insert at arbitrary position — the shift is $O(n)$ every time, no compensation.
  • multiset::erase(value) when the value appears $k$ times — $O(\log n + k)$.
  • string::substr — a fresh allocation of size $O(\text{length})$ every call.

docs.title: Complexity of STL Operations
docs.text:
The containers and algorithms you use constantly have specific asymptotic costs that you must know by heart. Here is the reference table for the operations that matter:

Operation Complexity Notes v[i] access on vector $O(1)$ two pointer dereferences v.push_back amortized $O(1)$ 2× growth v.pop_back $O(1)$ v.insert(v.begin()+k, x) $O(n)$ shifts all elements after $k$ v.erase(v.begin()+k) $O(n)$ shifts all elements after $k$ v.clear() $O(n)$ destroys $n$ elements v.resize(k) $O(n)$ fills or destroys $n$ elements sort(v.begin(), v.end()) $O(n \log n)$ introsort lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x) $O(\log n)$ requires random-access iterators set::find(x) / set::insert(x) $O(\log n)$ red-black tree set::lower_bound(x) (member) $O(\log n)$ uses tree structure std::lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x) on a set $O(n)$ linear scan — the classic trap set::erase(x) $O(\log n)$ multiset::erase(x) $O(\log n + k)$ where $k$ = count erases all copies multiset::erase(iterator) $O(\log n)$ erases one map::operator[] $O(\log n)$ inserts if missing map::find(x) $O(\log n)$ unordered_map::find / insert average $O(1)$, worst $O(n)$ anti-hash vulnerability priority_queue::push / pop $O(\log n)$ sift-up / sift-down priority_queue::top $O(1)$ queue/stack push/pop $O(1)$ deque push_front/push_back/pop $O(1)$ amortized nth_element $O(n)$ average introselect partial_sort(first, mid, last) $O(n \log k)$ $k$ = distance from first to mid binary_search(begin, end, x) $O(\log n)$ requires sorted accumulate $O(n)$ unique(begin, end) $O(n)$ only collapses consecutive duplicates next_permutation $O(n)$ per call total $n!$ calls to enumerate all s.find(t) on string $O(\|s\| \cdot \|t\|)$ worst naive matching

The two most-tested traps in this table are the set::lower_bound trap (a $O(\log n)$ operation becomes $O(n)$ if you call the free function) and the multiset::erase(value) trap (erases all copies, not one). Both have been the cause of TLEs and WAs on countless contest submissions.

docs.title: Mapping Constraints to Complexities
docs.text:
The judge's constraint on $n$ (usually stated in the problem as $1 \le n \le 10^5$, etc.) is the single most useful signal about the intended complexity. Reverse-engineer it:

Constraint on $n$ Intended complexity Why $n \le 10$ $O(n!)$, $O(n^n)$ $10! = 3.6 \cdot 10^6$, brute force fits $n \le 20$ $O(2^n)$, $O(n \cdot 2^n)$ $2^{20} \approx 10^6$, subset enumeration fits $n \le 100$ $O(n^3)$ $10^6$, Floyd–Warshall territory $n \le 500$ $O(n^3)$ tight, $O(n^2 \log n)$ preferred $1.25 \cdot 10^8$ borderline $n \le 10^3$ $O(n^2)$ $10^6$ comfortable $n \le 10^4$ $O(n^2)$ tight, prefer $O(n \log n)$ $10^8$ near the limit $n \le 10^5$ $O(n \log n)$ required $n^2 = 10^{10}$ impossible $n \le 10^6$ $O(n \log n)$ tight, prefer $O(n)$ need efficient I/O $n \le 10^7$ $O(n)$ with small constant tight on I/O, use custom reader $n \le 10^9$ $O(\log n)$, $O(\sqrt{n})$ cannot loop over $n$ $n \le 10^{12}$ $O(\sqrt{n})$ or $O(n^{1/3})$ number-theoretic techniques $n \le 10^{18}$ $O(\log n)$, $O(\log^2 n)$ matrix exponentiation, binary lifting

The reverse question is equally useful: given a complexity and a time limit, what is the largest $n$ you can afford? The answer depends on the constant factor, which you can approximate:

Time budget $O(1)$ $O(\log n)$ $O(n)$ $O(n \log n)$ $O(n^2)$ $O(n^3)$ $O(2^n)$ 1 s (modern) any $n$ any $n$ $\sim 10^8$ $\sim 5 \cdot 10^6$ $\sim 10^4$ $\sim 500$ $\sim 25$ 1 s (older) any $n$ any $n$ $\sim 10^7$ $\sim 10^6$ $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$ $\sim 200$ $\sim 22$ 2 s (modern) any $n$ any $n$ $\sim 2 \cdot 10^8$ $\sim 10^7$ $\sim 1.5 \cdot 10^4$ $\sim 600$ $\sim 26$

The "modern" column assumes a typical 2024-era Codeforces/AtCoder machine: ~$5 \cdot 10^8$ simple operations per second for the $O(n)$ column, and correspondingly faster for other complexities. The "older" column is a conservative assumption for judges running on weaker hardware or with heavier per-operation overhead.

docs.title: Real-World Benchmarks
docs.text:
The $10^8$ operations-per-second rule of thumb is useful but crude. Here are measured approximate throughputs on typical 2024-era judges under -O2 with <bits/stdc++.h> and sync_with_stdio(false):

Operation Approximate rate Time for $n = 10^6$ int arithmetic in a tight loop $\sim 10^9$/s 1 ms Array/vector access, sequential $\sim 5 \cdot 10^8$/s 2 ms vector::push_back (with reserve) $\sim 5 \cdot 10^8$/s 2 ms vector::push_back (without reserve) $\sim 10^8$/s 10 ms std::sort on random ints $\sim 5 \cdot 10^7 \cdot \log_2 n$/s ~100 ms lower_bound on vector<int> $\sim 2 \cdot 10^7$/s 50 ms set::insert $\sim 3 \cdot 10^6$/s 330 ms unordered_map::insert $\sim 10^7$/s 100 ms priority_queue::push + pop $\sim 5 \cdot 10^6$/s 200 ms string concatenation (single char) $\sim 10^7$/s 100 ms cout << x (with fast I/O) $\sim 10^7$/s 100 ms cout << x (without sync_with_stdio(false)) $\sim 10^6$/s 1 s cin >> x (with fast I/O) $\sim 5 \cdot 10^7$/s 20 ms cin >> x (without sync_with_stdio(false)) $\sim 10^6$/s 1 s

The factor of 50× between cin with and without fast I/O, and the factor of 10× between set::insert and unordered_map::insert, are the kind of gaps that Big-O hides — both pairs have "the same" asymptotic for a single operation, but the constants differ enormously. This is why the practical rules (fast I/O, sorted vector over set, custom hash for unordered_map) matter as much as the asymptotic analysis itself.

docs.title: Space-Time Tradeoffs
docs.text:
Complexity analysis applies to memory as well as time, and in CP the two are often exchangeable:

Precomputation for faster queries. The classic example is prefix sums:

// O(n) precompute, O(1) per query
vector<long long> pref(n + 1, 0);
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) pref[i + 1] = pref[i] + a[i];
long long range_sum(int l, int r) { return pref[r + 1] - pref[l]; }

// vs O(1) precompute, O(r - l) per query
long long range_sum_naive(int l, int r) {
    long long s = 0;
    for (int i = l; i <= r; ++i) s += a[i];
    return s;
}

If you have $q = 10^5$ queries, the precomputed version is $10^5 \cdot O(1) = 10^5$ operations; the naive version is $10^5 \cdot 10^5 = 10^{10}$ — a TLE by four orders of magnitude. The price is $O(n)$ extra memory, which is negligible.

Memoization for overlapping subproblems. Naive Fibonacci is $O(\phi^n)$; memoized is $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space. The price of a hash table or array turns an exponential algorithm into a linear one — the foundational tradeoff of dynamic programming.

Sparse tables for range queries. For static range-min queries, a sparse table takes $O(n \log n)$ precomputation and $O(n \log n)$ memory, but answers any query in $O(1)$. The naive approach is $O(n)$ precomputation and $O(r-l)$ per query. For $10^5$ queries on $10^5$ elements, the sparse table is 50× faster at the cost of ~5× memory.

Hash tables for lookup. An unordered_map uses roughly 2× the memory of a sorted vector of pairs, but gives average $O(1)$ lookup instead of $O(\log n)$. For $10^7$ lookups, this is a factor of ~20 in time.

The general principle: spend memory to save time, as long as you stay within the memory limit. Typical CP memory limits are 256 MB or 512 MB; a $10^6$-element int array is 4 MB, and a $10^7$-element array is 40 MB. Both fit comfortably. A $10^8$-element array at 4 bytes each is 400 MB — over the limit on most judges, so $10^8$ is usually the practical ceiling for a single array.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
A checklist for when complexity analysis or its application goes wrong:

  1. Assuming unordered_map is $O(1)$ worst case — it is average $O(1)$, worst $O(n)$. Codeforces anti-hash tests exploit this; use a custom hash.
  2. Calling std::lower_bound on a set — it is $O(n)$, not $O(\log n)$. Use s.lower_bound(x).
  3. Forgetting accumulate(..., 0) accumulates in int — use 0LL for long long sums.
  4. Naive Fibonacci as "$O(2^n)$" — it is $\Theta(\phi^n)$; a factor of ~4000 more efficient than the bound suggests at $n = 40$.
  5. Confusing $10^5$ with 10^5 — the latter is 15 in C++. Use 100'000.
  6. Estimating time from operations without considering constants — 10^8 set::insert takes 30 s, not 0.1 s, because each insert is $O(\log n)$ with a large constant.
  7. Ignoring I/O cost — $10^6$ numbers read with default cin take 1 s on its own; always use sync_with_stdio(false) and cin.tie(nullptr).
  8. Assuming vector::erase is $O(1)$ — it is $O(n)$ in the middle of the vector, because subsequent elements shift.
  9. Forgetting to count the recursion stack — a DFS on a $10^5$-node path uses $O(n)$ stack, which can overflow 8 MB on some judges.
  10. Assuming $O(n^2)$ is fine for $n = 10^4$ — it is $10^8$, which is borderline on 1 s limits. Prefer $O(n \log n)$ when possible.
  11. Underestimating $O(n \log n)$ for $n = 10^6$ — $10^6 \cdot 20 = 2 \cdot 10^7$, fine; but with a large constant (like set-based operations), it becomes 10 s.
  12. Confusing "amortized $O(1)$" with "worst-case $O(1)$" — push_back can be $O(n)$ for a single call; if that single call is in a hot loop with interrupts or time limits, it matters.
  13. Ignoring the constant factor for small $n$ — an $O(n^2)$ algorithm with tiny constant may beat $O(n \log n)$ with large constant for $n \le 100$. Measure if in doubt.
  14. Assuming sort is $O(n \log n)$ worst case — std::sort is introsort, which is $O(n \log n)$ worst case (heapsort fallback), unlike naive quicksort which is $O(n^2)$ worst case.
  15. Estimating constraints from $n$ alone — $n \le 10^5$ with $m$ also up to $10^5$ edges means the algorithm must be $O((n + m) \log n)$ or better for graph problems, not just $O(n \log n)$.
  16. Ignoring the total operations across multiple test cases — $t$ test cases each with $n = 10^4$ requires the algorithm to be fast per test case; a $10^4 \cdot 10^4 = 10^8$ total is fine, but $10^4 \cdot 10^6 = 10^{10}$ is not.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Asymptotic notation is about growth, not exact counts. Big-O is an upper bound; $\Theta$ is the tight one; $\Omega$ is a lower bound. Use $\Theta$ when you mean "exactly this complexity".
  • The $n$-limit table is the most useful tool in your kit. $n \le 10^5$ means $O(n \log n)$ is required, $O(n^2)$ is impossible. Read the constraints before choosing an algorithm.
  • Sequential adds, nested multiplies, halved/doubled loops are logarithmic. Recursion via recurrence relations; Master Theorem for divide-and-conquer.
  • Naive Fibonacci is $\Theta(\phi^n)$, not $O(2^n)$. The bound $O(2^n)$ is correct but not tight, and the difference matters numerically.
  • Amortized $O(1)$ is not $O(1)$. push_back can be $O(n)$ on a single call, but averages $O(1)$. Understand the difference.
  • unordered_map is average $O(1)$, worst $O(n)$. Codeforces adversarial tests exploit this. Use a custom hash if you rely on hashing.
  • set::lower_bound is $O(\log n)$; std::lower_bound on a set is $O(n)$. This is the most-tested STL complexity trap.
  • The $10^8$ ops/s rule is a starting point, not a law. Constants vary by 10–50× across operations. Measure, or use the benchmark table in this article.
  • Spend memory to save time, up to the memory limit. Prefix sums, sparse tables, memoization — these are the fundamental space-time tradeoffs of CP.
  • Always count the recursion stack. $O(n)$ recursion depth is $O(n)$ memory; on a 8 MB stack, that means a few $10^5$ frames maximum.

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text:
• CSES — Maximum Subarray Sum — Kadane's $O(n)$ vs. naive $O(n^2)$ vs. $O(n^3)$; the problem shows why $n \le 10^5$ rules out the slower versions.
  • CSES — Sum of Two Values — two-pointer $O(n \log n)$ after sort vs. $O(n^2)$ double loop; $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ forces the sorted approach.
  • CSES — Building Teams — bipartite check via BFS, $O(n + m)$; a good drill for reading the constraints as $O((n+m) \log n)$ for the full problem.
  • Codeforces 4A — Watermelon — trivial $O(1)$; the point is recognizing that no complexity analysis is needed.
  • CSES — Creating Strings — $n \le 8$ permits $O(n!)$ enumeration via next_permutation; the constraint is the hint.
  • CSES — Subset Sums — a problem where $n \le 10^5$ rules out $O(n \cdot \text{sum})$ subset-sum DP and forces an $O(1)$ mathematical construction; a good example of constraints reverse-engineering the intended solution.
  • Codeforces 1611E1 — Escape The Maze (easy version) — BFS on a tree, $O(n)$; contrast with the hard version, where a slower approach TLEs at the larger constraint.

docs.title: Arrays and Vectors
docs.text:
An array is a contiguous block of memory holding elements of the same type. That one sentence is the reason arrays dominate competitive programming: contiguous memory means the CPU can prefetch, vectorize, and cache efficiently, and index arithmetic compiles to a single mov instruction. Almost every efficient data structure you will meet — segment trees, Fenwick trees, sparse tables, DP tables, adjacency lists, union-find — is built on top of an array. If you understand how arrays and vectors work at the memory level, every algorithm downstream becomes easier to reason about; if you treat them as opaque boxes, subtle bugs (overflow, invalidation, shallow copies) will follow you through the entire course.

This article covers both std::array-style static arrays and std::vector, with a focus on the parts that matter in contests: initialization guarantees, stack vs heap, capacity growth, iterator invalidation, and cache behavior. Those are the areas where nearly every WA/TLE comes from.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Introduction to C++ — compilation, -O2, the CP template.
  • I/O and Data Types — int vs long long, size_t, signed/unsigned traps.
  • Conditionals and Loops — loop idioms, off-by-one hazards.

Throughout we assume the CP template:

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    // ...
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Arrays as Contiguous Memory
docs.text:
Before writing any code, internalize this mental model:

int a[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};

Address:   0x1000  0x1004  0x1008  0x100c  0x1010
Value:       10      20      30      40      50
Index:        0       1       2       3       4

The address of a[i] is a + i * sizeof(int). Two consequences follow:

  1. Indexing is $O(1)$ — a single multiply-add, then a memory load.
  2. Accesses to nearby indices hit the same cache line (typically 64 bytes = 16 ints). Iterating left to right is much faster than iterating in a scattered order, and vastly faster than traversing a linked structure.

These two facts are why the array is the workhorse of competitive programming. A std::map has the same $O(\log n)$ asymptotic as binary search on a sorted array, but the array's constant factor is typically 10–50× smaller because it never leaves a cache line.

docs.title: Static Arrays
docs.text: A static array's size is known at compile time. In CP, "static" usually means two things: declared at global scope (fast zero-initialization, plentiful memory) or declared locally with a compile-time constant size.

docs.title: Declaration and initialization
docs.text:
int arr[5];                 // Uninitialized (if local) — contains garbage
int fixed[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
int partial[5] = {1, 2};    // {1, 2, 0, 0, 0} — the rest are zero
int zeros[5] = {};          // {0, 0, 0, 0, 0} — the canonical way

The pitfall hiding in the first line is initialization guarantees differ by storage duration:

  • Global or static arrays are zero-initialized by the OS. int cnt[100]; at file scope starts as all zeros.
  • Local arrays are not initialized. int cnt[100]; inside main contains whatever was on the stack — often zeros in practice, but undefined behavior to read. Under -O2, the compiler may assume uninitialized values are never read, and eliminate code that would have "read" them.

This is why competitive programming templates almost universally use global arrays for large state: they are guaranteed zero-initialized, allocated in the static data segment (not the 8 MB stack), and accessible from any function without passing pointers.

constexpr int MAXN = 200'005;
int parent[MAXN];     // global — zero-initialized, 200005 * 4 bytes = ~800 KB, no stack cost
long long dp[MAXN];   // global — fits the entire DP without heap allocations

docs.title: std::array — the modern C++ alternative
docs.text:
Since C++11, std::array<T, N> is the standard-library type for fixed-size arrays. It is stack-allocated, size is part of the type, and it supports .size(), iterators, and STL algorithms:

array<int, 5> a = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
a.size();          // 5, always — no pointer decay
a.fill(0);         // reset all elements
sort(a.begin(), a.end());

In CP, std::array is useful when you need STL compatibility without heap allocation — e.g., as a key type in map, or as the return value of a function that would otherwise decay to a pointer. For pure CP use, though, plain C arrays declared globally remain the most common choice.

docs.title: Stack overflow with large local arrays
docs.text:
The stack is typically 8 MB (Linux default). A local int a[1'000'000]; is 4 MB — dangerously close to the limit once you add the call chain. A local int a[10'000'000]; is 40 MB and will crash with a segmentation fault or, worse, produce garbage under -O2 because the runtime did not catch the overflow.

The fix is simple and habitual: declare any array larger than ~100 KB at global scope.

// BAD: 4 MB on the stack — dangerous
int main() {
    int dp[1'000'000];
    // ...
}

// GOOD: 4 MB in the static data segment — safe, zero-initialized
constexpr int MAXN = 1'000'000;
int dp[MAXN];   // global

int main() {
    // ...
}

If you must have a local array whose size is enormous, use vector<int> instead — it allocates on the heap. If you genuinely need a stack array for performance, increase the stack size locally with ulimit -s unlimited (this affects your machine, not the judge — never rely on it in the final submission).

docs.title: Multi-dimensional arrays — memory layout matters
docs.text:
A 2D array int mat[R][C] is not an array of arrays in the general sense; it is one contiguous block of R * C ints, stored row-major:

int mat[2][3] = {{1,2,3}, {4,5,6}};

Address:  0x1000 0x1004 0x1008 0x100c 0x1010 0x1014
Value:      1      2      3      4      5      6
Logical:  [0][0] [0][1] [0][2] [1][0] [1][1] [1][2]

The address of mat[i][j] is base + (i * C + j) * sizeof(int). Two consequences:

  1. Iterating row by row matches memory order — the cache happily prefetches the entire next row.
  2. Iterating column by column jumps C * sizeof(int) bytes at each step — every access is a potential cache miss. For a $1000 \times 1000$ array, column-major traversal can be 5–10× slower than row-major:
// FAST — row-major traversal matches memory layout
for (int i = 0; i < R; ++i)
    for (int j = 0; j < C; ++j)
        sum += mat[i][j];

// SLOW — column-major traversal, cache-hostile
for (int j = 0; j < C; ++j)
    for (int i = 0; i < R; ++i)
        sum += mat[i][j];

How big can a 2D array be? With a 256 MB limit, you can fit $\lfloor 256 \cdot 10^6 / 4 \rfloor = 64 \cdot 10^6$ ints. That is a $8000 \times 8000$ grid, not $10^3 \times 10^3$ as some tutorials incorrectly state. The practical limit depends on the memory limit and element size, not on any "row × column" threshold. Compute R * C * sizeof(T) and compare it to the limit before assuming a matrix "won't fit".

docs.title: std::vector — the dynamic array
docs.text: std::vector<T> is a heap-allocated, dynamically-sized, contiguous array. For competitive programming, it is the default choice for anything whose size is read at runtime. Its overhead over a raw array is one pointer (data()), one size counter, and one capacity counter — 24 bytes on 64-bit, allocated on the heap.

docs.title: Construction — five idioms to know
docs.text:
vector<int> v1;                  // empty, capacity 0
vector<int> v2(5);               // five 0s
vector<int> v3(5, 10);           // {10, 10, 10, 10, 10}
vector<int> v4 = {1, 2, 3, 4};   // list initialization
vector<int> v5(v4.begin(), v4.end()); // copy of v4

All five are common in CP, but the second one has a trap:

vector<int> v(-1) is a bomb. The constructor's parameter is size_t (unsigned). -1 is converted to SIZE_MAX ≈ 1.8 · 10^{19}, the vector tries to allocate that many ints, and you get std::bad_alloc or a hard crash. If a variable that should be non-negative becomes negative, the bug manifests as a memory error rather than a logical wrong answer — much harder to debug. Compile with -Wall -Wextra; GCC warns about the sign conversion for literals.

docs.title: push_back vs emplace_back
docs.text:
Both append an element in amortized $O(1)$. The distinction only matters for non-trivial types:

vector<pair<int, int>> vp;
vp.push_back({1, 2});           // constructs a temporary pair, then moves it
vp.emplace_back(1, 2);          // constructs the pair in place — one fewer move

vector<string> vs;
vs.push_back("hello");          // temporary, then move — usually optimized away
vs.emplace_back(10, 'a');       // constructs "aaaaaaaaaa" in place — no temporary

For int, long long, double, and small structs, the difference is negligible and push_back is clearer. For containers of containers, emplace_back can save measurable time. In DP-heavy code where you build arrays of pairs millions of times, emplace_back is the right habit.

docs.title: size vs capacity vs reserve vs resize
docs.text:
This is the most important conceptual difference in vector. Understanding it eliminates both TLEs and memory bugs:

  • size() — number of elements currently in the vector.
  • capacity() — number of elements the current allocation can hold without reallocating. capacity() >= size() always.
  • reserve(n) — ensures capacity() >= n. Does not change size(). If called before a series of push_back, it eliminates all reallocations.
  • resize(n) — changes size() to exactly n. If n > size(), new elements are value-initialized (0 for int, "" for string); if n < size(), elements are destroyed.
vector<int> v;
v.reserve(1'000'000);       // capacity is now >= 1e6, size is still 0
for (int i = 0; i < 1'000'000; ++i) v.push_back(i);   // zero reallocations

v.resize(500'000);          // size is now 500k — half the elements destroyed

The 10^5 bug (seriously). In C++, 10^5 is bitwise XOR, not exponentiation. 10 ^ 5 equals 15, not 100000. So a line like

v.reserve(10^5);                         // reserves 15 elements — useless!
for (int i = 0; i < 10^5; ++i) { ... }   // loops 15 times, not 100000!

silently loops the wrong number of times and reserves the wrong amount of memory. This is a real, common WA pattern in CP code. Always write 100000, 100'000, or 1e5 (which is a double and converts to int cleanly — int(1e5) == 100000, but be aware that 1e9 as a double is exact while 1e10 is not).

docs.title: How vector grows — and why iterators are invalidated
docs.text:
When push_back needs space and size == capacity, the vector allocates a new buffer of typically 2× the current capacity, moves all elements, and frees the old buffer. This is amortized $O(1)$ because the geometric growth spreads the reallocation cost across all insertions.

The consequence is iterator invalidation:

After any push_back that triggers reallocation, all iterators, pointers, and references into the vector are invalidated.

vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3};
int* p = &v[0];
v.push_back(4);          // may reallocate — p is now dangling
cout << *p;              // UNDEFINED BEHAVIOR

The classic bug pattern is modifying a vector inside a range-for:

for (int x : v) {
    if (x < 0) v.push_back(-x);   // UB — invalidates the implicit iterator
}

If you need to append while iterating, use an explicit index and process the appended elements in a second pass, or collect the additions in a separate vector first:

vector<int> to_add;
for (int x : v) if (x < 0) to_add.push_back(-x);
v.insert(v.end(), to_add.begin(), to_add.end());

reserve() before a loop with push_back avoids all reallocations and the invalidation problem entirely:

v.reserve(n);
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) v.push_back(compute(i));

docs.title: Element access
docs.text:
vector<int> v = {10, 20, 30, 40};

v[0]            // no bounds check — O(1), the workhorse in CP
v.at(0)         // bounds check — throws std::out_of_range, ~2x slower
v.front()       // v[0]
v.back()        // v[size()-1]
v.data()        // raw pointer — useful for C API interop and scanf

For competitive programming, prefer v[i] — the bounds check in .at() is a real cost in hot loops, and correctness is guaranteed by your algorithm. Use .at() only while debugging an out-of-bounds bug: compile with -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG and every v[i] out-of-bounds becomes a runtime error, catching the bug immediately.

Empty-vector traps. v.back() and v.pop_back() on an empty vector are undefined behavior. v[v.size() - 1] wraps to v[SIZE_MAX] and crashes. Always guard with if (!v.empty()) before back/pop.

docs.title: Iterating — four idiomatic forms
docs.text:
vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};

// 1. Index — needed when you also want the position
for (int i = 0; i < (int)v.size(); ++i)
    cout << v[i] << " ";

// 2. Range-based — cleanest for read-only iteration
for (const int& x : v)
    cout << x << " ";

// 3. Iterator — needed for STL algorithms that return iterators
for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it)
    cout << *it << " ";

// 4. Reverse iterator — for backward passes
for (auto it = v.rbegin(); it != v.rend(); ++it)
    cout << *it << " ";

Prefer the range-based form for anything read-only, with const auto& for non-trivial element types. For write access, use auto&:

for (int& x : v) x *= 2;               // modifies v — cheap, int is a primitive
for (const string& s : vs) cout << s;  // no copies
for (string s : vs)        /* BUG */ ; // copies every string

The signed/unsigned trap resurfaces with .size():

for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i)         // warns with -Wsign-compare; safe only if i >= 0
for (int i = 0; i < (int)v.size(); ++i)    // explicit cast — recommended
for (size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i)      // fully unsigned — also fine

docs.title: STL Algorithms on Ranges
docs.text: <algorithm> and <numeric> provide operations that operate on any iterator range — vector, std::array, C arrays, string, deque. These are implemented by experts and are usually faster than hand-rolled equivalents because the compiler can vectorize them.

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
sort(v.begin(), v.end());                            // ascending, O(n log n)
sort(v.begin(), v.end(), greater<int>());            // descending
sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) {          // custom order
    return (a % 10) < (b % 10);                      // sort by last digit
});

The comparator must define a strict weak ordering. return a <= b; is a bug — it says a comes before itself, which sort does not expect, and the standard says the behavior is undefined. It usually looks fine on small inputs and crashes or loops on large ones. Always use <, never <=.

For pairs and tuples, sort uses lexicographic order by default — pair<int, int> sorts by first, then by second. This is why the pair type is so convenient for sorting events, coordinates, or anything with a natural tiebreak.

docs.title: unique — the shift-and-return idiom
docs.text:
unique(begin, end) does not remove elements. It shifts the first of each run of equal elements to the front, and returns an iterator past the last unique element. To actually remove duplicates:

sort(v.begin(), v.end());                              // sort first — required
v.erase(unique(v.begin(), v.end()), v.end());          // then erase tail

If you call unique without sorting, only consecutive duplicates are collapsed — which is almost never what you want.

docs.title: Binary search — lower_bound, upper_bound, binary_search
docs.text:
These require the range to be sorted (by the same comparator). They return iterators, not indices:

sort(v.begin(), v.end());

bool found = binary_search(v.begin(), v.end(), 5);

// First position where v[i] >= 5
int lo = lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), 5) - v.begin();

// First position where v[i] > 5
int hi = upper_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), 5) - v.begin();

// Count of elements equal to 5
int cnt = hi - lo;

The - v.begin() conversion to index is the idiomatic way to use these in CP. lower_bound on an unsorted range is undefined behavior — not just "wrong result", actually UB, because the algorithm uses the comparator's transitivity assumption to narrow the search.

docs.title: iota, fill, accumulate, count, find, reverse
docs.text:
#include <numeric>

vector<int> v(n);
iota(v.begin(), v.end(), 0);           // v = {0, 1, 2, ..., n-1}
fill(v.begin(), v.end(), -1);          // set all elements
long long total = accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL); // 0LL forces long long accumulation

int c = count(v.begin(), v.end(), 5);
auto it = find(v.begin(), v.end(), 9);
reverse(v.begin(), v.end());

accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0) on an int vector accumulates in int — the result overflows at $2^{31}$, silently. Use 0LL to force 64-bit accumulation. This is one of the most common silent-WA patterns in contest code.

docs.title: 2D Structures
docs.text: Two idioms for 2D data, with different tradeoffs.

docs.title: Nested vectors — vector<vector<int>>
docs.text:
int n, m; cin >> n >> m;
vector<vector<int>> grid(n, vector<int>(m));
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
    for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j)
        cin >> grid[i][j];

Clear, natural syntax, grid[i][j] works as expected. The downside is that each inner vector is a separate heap allocation, so rows are not contiguous with each other. For $n = 10^5$ rows of size 1, this is 100,000 separate allocations — a measurable constant-factor cost. For moderate $n, m$, it is fine; the clarity usually wins.

docs.title: Flat vector — one contiguous buffer
docs.text:
int n, m; cin >> n >> m;
vector<int> grid(n * m);
auto idx = [m](int i, int j) { return i * m + j; };
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
    for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j)
        cin >> grid[idx(i, j)];

One allocation, perfect cache locality, and .data() gives you a raw pointer if needed. The downside is the explicit index arithmetic — a source of subtle bugs (i * m + j vs i * n + j) if you are not careful. Use flat vectors for large grids ($n \cdot m \ge 10^6$) or when you will do row-wise passes; use nested for readability otherwise.

docs.title: Fixed 2D array at global scope
docs.text:
For matrices with compile-time dimensions, the simplest option is often the best:

constexpr int MAXN = 1'005;
int mat[MAXN][MAXN];   // global — zero-initialized, one allocation

This is a single contiguous block of MAXN * MAXN * 4 bytes — for MAXN = 1005, about 4 MB. Fits comfortably under any memory limit and is fast enough that grid DP, BFS on grids, and prefix-sum matrices rarely need more.

docs.title: Global arrays for large state
docs.text:
constexpr int MAXN = 200'005;
int parent[MAXN];
long long dist[MAXN];
int visited[MAXN];

Global = zero-initialized, no stack limit, no allocation overhead. The default choice for anything above ~10^4 elements.

docs.title: Prefix sums — $O(1)$ range-sum queries after $O(n)$ preprocessing
docs.text:
vector<long long> pref(n + 1, 0);
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) pref[i + 1] = pref[i] + a[i];
// sum of a[l..r] inclusive:
long long s = pref[r + 1] - pref[l];

Use long long for the prefix array — the running sum of $10^5$ values near $10^9$ overflows int.

docs.title: Adjacency list for graphs
docs.text:
vector<vector<int>> adj(n);
for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
    int u, v; cin >> u >> v; --u; --v;
    adj[u].push_back(v);
    adj[v].push_back(u);   // omit for directed graphs
}

This is the standard graph representation in CP: $O(V + E)$ memory and $O(\text{deg}(u))$ neighbor iteration. Most graph algorithms are written against it directly.

docs.title: DP table as a vector
docs.text:
vector<long long> dp(n + 1, INF);
dp[0] = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
    for (int j : moves[i])
        dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[j] + cost(j, i));

For DP with only previous-row dependency, a rolling array saves memory:

vector<long long> prev(m + 1, 0), curr(m + 1, 0);
for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    for (int j = 0; j <= m; ++j) curr[j] = ...;
    swap(prev, curr);   // O(1) — no copying
}

docs.title: bitset for boolean arrays
docs.text:
vector<bool> is a bit-packed specialization with proxy references — bool& does not work, &v[i] does not compile, and non-adjacent elements share bytes. For a dense boolean array, use std::bitset instead:

bitset<200'005> visited;    // 25 KB, all zeros
visited[42] = 1;
visited.count();            // number of set bits
visited.flip();             // complement

bitset operations (&, |, ^, <<, >>) run on entire words in parallel — a bitset<10^6> shift is ~15,000× faster than a loop. This is the foundation of many "small boolean state" optimizations in DP and reachability.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
Rough throughput of array- and vector-based operations on typical judge hardware with -O2:

Operation Operations per second v[i] (sequential, cached) $\sim 10^9$ push_back with reserve $\sim 10^8 - 10^9$ push_back without reserve $\sim 10^7 - 10^8$ (reallocation dominates) sort $\sim 10^7 \cdot \log n$ comparisons lower_bound (random access) $\sim 10^7$ per second std::map operation $\sim 10^6 - 10^7$ unordered_map operation $\sim 10^6 - 10^7$

Key guidance:

  • reserve when the final size is known. For a vector of $10^6$ elements, reserve before the push_back loop can save 20 reallocations and 2× total memory churn.
  • Contiguous beats tree-shaped. Sorting a vector and binary-searching it is often 10× faster than using std::map or std::set for the same logical queries, because the vector never leaves cache. Reach for map only when you need ordered insertion/deletion interleaved with queries.
  • Small integer keys can use arrays as hash maps. A vector<int> cnt(MAXV) indexed by value is $O(1)$ with a tiny constant — beats unordered_map unless MAXV is large and sparse. This is the "direct-address table" trick and is everywhere in CP.
  • Flat 2D arrays beat nested vectors for large grids. For $1000 \times 1000$, the difference is typically 2–3×.
  • Iterate in memory order. Row-major for row-major arrays; forward for forward-access containers. The cache loves this.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
A checklist to run whenever your array- or vector-based solution WAs or TLEs:

  1. 10^5 instead of 100000 — ^ is XOR, not power. 10^5 == 15, not 100000. Write 100'000 or 1e5.
  2. Local arrays are uninitialized — global arrays are zero, local ones are garbage. Declare large state at global scope.
  3. Stack overflow from large local arrays — a local int a[10^6] is 4 MB; the stack is typically 8 MB. Move it to global.
  4. vector<int> v(-1) — constructor parameter is size_t, -1 becomes SIZE_MAX, crash.
  5. v.back() or v.pop_back() on an empty vector — UB; guard with !v.empty().
  6. v.size() - 1 on an empty vector — wraps to SIZE_MAX; guard.
  7. Iterators invalidated by push_back — reference/pointer/iterator into the vector is dangling after a reallocation. Use reserve or index-based access.
  8. Modifying a container inside a range-for — the same invalidation, hidden.
  9. accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0) on an int vector — accumulates in int, overflows silently. Use 0LL.
  10. unique without sort — only removes consecutive duplicates.
  11. unique without erase — only shifts elements; the container still has n elements.
  12. lower_bound on an unsorted range — UB, not just a wrong result.
  13. Comparator return a <= b — not a strict weak ordering; UB. Use <.
  14. v.at() in a hot loop — bounds check costs 1.5–2×; use v[i] unless debugging.
  15. Passing a vector by value — copies the entire buffer. Use const vector<int>&.
  16. vector<bool> misuse — proxy references, bool& does not compile, &v[i] invalid. Use bitset or vector<char>.
  17. Column-major traversal of a row-major 2D array — 5–10× slowdown from cache misses.
  18. i * m + j vs i * n + j in flat-vector indexing — a silent way to read wrong cells.
  19. Signed/unsigned comparison with .size() — safe only if the counter is always $\ge 0$; use (int)v.size() when in doubt.
  20. sort on a range of size 0 — fine (no-op), but v.front() on an empty vector is UB; guard.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• An array is contiguous memory; indexing is $O(1)$ address arithmetic, and sequential access exploits the cache. Every fast data structure in CP rests on this.
  • Global arrays are zero-initialized and escape the 8 MB stack. Default to global for anything larger than ~$10^4$ elements.
  • vector is the default container for runtime-sized data. Use reserve to eliminate reallocations; resize changes size, reserve changes capacity.
  • push_back may invalidate all iterators into the vector. Guard with reserve, or use index-based access.
  • The comparator in sort must be strict (<, not <=). The result of violating this is undefined behavior.
  • accumulate accumulates in the initial value's type — use 0LL for long long results.
  • 2D: nested vector<vector<int>> for clarity, flat vector<int> for large grids. Row-major traversal matches memory layout.
  • Reach for arrays and bitset before map whenever possible — contiguous memory is orders of magnitude faster than tree-shaped containers.
  • Write 100'000, not 10^5. The XOR bug is silent and lethal.

docs.title: Conditionals and Loops
docs.text:
Every algorithm you will ever write in competitive programming is built from three things: decisions (which branch to take), repetition (how many times to do something), and data (what to do it on). This article is about the first two. Master them and the third — arrays, graphs, trees — becomes mechanical. Get them subtly wrong and no amount of clever algorithmic thinking will save you: a single off-by-one in a loop bound or a missing break turns a correct $O(n \log n)$ idea into a WA.

The goal here is not just to list syntax. It is to build the reflexes you need under contest pressure: which construct to reach for, and — more importantly — which reflex will bite you when you are not paying attention.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Introduction to C++ — compilation, -O2, the CP template.
  • I/O and Data Types — int vs long long, signed/unsigned traps, size_t.

Throughout, we assume the standard template:

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    // ...
    return 0;
}

docs.title: if / else if / else — making decisions
docs.text:
An if statement asks a yes/no question about the current state of the program and picks a path. In competitive programming, conditionals are the glue between the mathematical core of a solution and its many edge cases: Is $n = 1$? Is the answer negative? Did we reach the target?

int x; cin >> x;
if (x > 0)        cout << "Positive\n";
else if (x < 0)   cout << "Negative\n";
else              cout << "Zero\n";

The key mental model is short-circuit evaluation and top-down matching. Conditions are tested in order; the first one that is true wins, and everything below is skipped. This is not just a control-flow detail — it is a performance tool. When a later condition is expensive (a map lookup, a string comparison, a geometric predicate), put the cheap ones first:

if (n == 0) { /* O(1) early exit */ }
else if (is_valid(grid)) { /* O(n·m) — only checked when necessary */ }

In CP, you will write if statements for three common roles:

  1. Guard clauses at the top — handle degenerate input immediately so the rest of the code can assume well-formed data.
  2. Classification — separate cases that need different algorithms (e.g., $n$ even vs odd, connected vs disconnected).
  3. Boundary checks inside loops — if (i + 1 < n && a[i] == a[i+1]) appears constantly in sliding-window and two-pointer solutions.

Best practice. Keep each condition small and named when it is not obvious. A line like if (x >= 0 && x < n && y >= 0 && y < m && !visited[x][y]) is fine; a line like if (a * b > c ^ d & e) is a bug you haven't found yet.

docs.title: The if (x = 5) pitfall — assignment vs comparison
docs.text:
int x = 3;
if (x = 5) { /* ... */ }   // assigns 5; condition is 5 (truthy); x becomes 5
if (x == 5) { /* ... */ }  // compares

Both lines compile. Only one does what you mean. This is the single most common typo in the history of C-family languages, and it has cost contestants countless submission penalties.

The defense is your compiler. Always compile with -Wall -Wextra. GCC emits -Wparentheses for this exact mistake and refuses to stay silent. If you are building a contest habit, make -Wall -Wextra muscle memory from day one. The alternative — the "Yoda condition" if (5 == x) — works but is unfashionable and hard to read; trust the compiler instead.

docs.title: The dangling else — a bug that looks correct
docs.text:
Consider:

if (a)
    if (b) cout << "ab\n";
    else   cout << "not b\n";   // which if does this belong to?

The else binds to the nearest unmatched if. Here, that is if (b), not if (a). So the code reads as "if a, then: (if b print 'ab', else print 'not b')" — but a human reader almost always misreads it as "(if a and b print 'ab', else print 'not b')". The two interpretations differ whenever a is false.

The fix is trivially reliable: always use braces. Not "when the body is more than one line" — always. Braces cost one keystroke and eliminate the entire class of dangling-else bugs. If you only adopt one habit from this article, adopt this one.

docs.title: The ternary operator ?: — compact decisions
docs.text:
The ternary operator produces a value based on a condition:

int mx = (a >= b) ? a : b;

It is essential in competitive programming for compact expressions that would otherwise require a temporary variable — dp[i] = (take) ? dp[i-1] + w : dp[i-1];, ans = (x < 0) ? -x : x; — but it has two real pitfalls.

Pitfall 1: parentheses around ?: when streaming. The precedence of << is higher than ?:, so

cout << a % 2 == 0 ? "Even" : "Odd";   // WRONG

is parsed as (cout << (a % 2 == 0)) ? "Even" : "Odd". The first part writes a bool to cout (printing 0 or 1) and evaluates to the stream, which is truthy in most contexts — you get nonsense output that looks like a number. Correct:

cout << (a % 2 == 0 ? "Even" : "Odd") << "\n";

Pitfall 2: hidden type conversions. The two branches of ?: are promoted to a common type, which is sometimes wider than expected:

long long x = (flag ? 1 : 0) * n;   // int result — can overflow before assignment
long long y = (flag ? 1LL : 0) * n; // long long — correct

The 1LL is not decoration; it makes the ternary return long long. This bites most often in dp[...] = (cond) ? 1 : MOD;-style lines where MOD is an int — the long long assignment does not rescue the overflow that already happened on the right side.

Readability rule. One level of ?: is fine. Two is hostile. Three is a bug waiting to happen — rewrite as explicit if-else and move on.

docs.title: switch — matching against constants
docs.text:
switch compares an integral expression against a list of compile-time constants. Because the values are known at compile time, the compiler can emit a jump table — $O(1)$ regardless of how many case labels there are, versus the $O(k)$ of an if-else chain with $k$ branches.

int op; cin >> op;
switch (op) {
    case 1: cout << "Addition\n";       break;
    case 2: cout << "Subtraction\n";    break;
    case 3: cout << "Multiplication\n"; break;
    default: cout << "Invalid\n";       break;
}

In competitive programming, switch shows up most often when parsing structured input: operations in a command stream ('L', 'R', 'U', 'D' for grid movement), direction codes, or query types in problems with mixed updates and reads. It is also common on enum values that represent a small set of states.

Pitfall 1: missing break → fall-through. Without break, execution continues into the next case:

switch (x) {
    case 1: do_one();
    case 2: do_two();   // runs for x == 1 as well!
}

Occasionally fall-through is intentional — for instance, grouping several cases under one handler:

case 'A': case 'E': case 'I': case 'O': case 'U':
    cout << "vowel\n";
    break;

In C++17 you can document intentional fall-through with [[fallthrough]]; to silence compiler warnings. For everything else, add the break.

Pitfall 2: declaring variables inside a case without braces. case labels do not introduce a new scope:

switch (x) {
    case 1:
        int y = 5;   // error: declaration crosses case label
        break;
}

Wrap the body in braces — case 1: { int y = 5; ... break; } — and the error disappears.

When to prefer if-else. For two or three non-contiguous values, if-else is at least as fast and far clearer. switch pays off when cases are dense (case 0..N) or when matching an enum, where the compiler can warn about missing cases (-Wswitch).

docs.title: Loops
docs.text: Loops are the heart of every algorithm. The three loop forms in C++ — for, while, and do-while — differ in how the termination condition is expressed, not in what they can compute. Choosing the wrong one rarely breaks your code, but it consistently makes it harder to reason about. Under contest pressure, that difficulty is where bugs live.

docs.title: for — when you know how many iterations
docs.text:
Use for when the iteration count is fixed or index-driven. Nearly every array and matrix traversal in competitive programming is a for loop, and so are most DP transitions (for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) for (int j = 0; j <= W; ++j) ...).

for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    // body
}

The three parts of the header are initialization (once), condition (before each iteration), and update (after each iteration). The subtlety that matters: continue in a for loop runs the update clause before the next condition check, unlike in while and do-while. This is the reason for is safer with continue, and why the common bug "infinite loop from continue in while" cannot happen in a for.

++i vs i++ — the myth. You will read in many tutorials that ++i is faster than i++. For int, this is false. With -O2, GCC and Clang emit identical assembly for both — the optimizer eliminates the temporary. The distinction matters only for iterator classes, where i++ must construct a copy of the old iterator. In competitive programming you almost never iterate by raw iterator; use whichever form you prefer. Do not waste mental energy micro-optimizing the wrong thing.

Scope of the loop variable. The counter int i declared in the header is scoped to the loop. This is usually what you want — but it means this fails:

for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { /* ... */ }
cout << i;   // error: i not declared

Declare the counter before the loop if you need it after.

The unsigned-counter infinite loop. This is one of the classic CP bugs:

for (unsigned i = n - 1; i >= 0; --i) {   // INFINITE if n == 0 or after i == 0
    // when i == 0, i-- wraps to UINT_MAX, which is >= 0
}

Two safe rewrites:

for (int i = (int)n - 1; i >= 0; --i) { /* ... */ }   // signed — exits at -1
for (int i = 0; i < (int)n; ++i)       { /* ... */ }   // forward direction

The rule: use int (or long long) for loop counters in competitive programming. Reserve unsigned for hashing and bit manipulation. The only exception is a range-based loop over .size(), where size_t is the natural type — and even then, cast when you need to iterate backwards.

The signed/unsigned comparison trap. v.size() returns size_t, which is unsigned. Comparing an int counter to it silently converts the counter to unsigned:

for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) { /* safe as long as i >= 0 always */ }

This is safe only because the loop starts at 0. If i ever goes negative, it wraps to a huge unsigned value and the condition becomes always true. The related expression v.size() - 1 is a live grenade — on an empty v, it wraps to SIZE_MAX. Two robust idioms:

for (int i = 0; i < (int)v.size(); ++i)    { /* ... */ }   // explicit cast, clearly signed
for (size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i)      { /* ... */ }   // fully unsigned domain

Both are fine. Pick one and use it consistently.

Overflow in the condition. for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i) with n == INT_MAX is undefined behavior — when i reaches INT_MAX, ++i overflows a signed int, and with -O2 the compiler is allowed to assume that never happens. The loop may terminate normally, may run forever, or may do something stranger. For n approaching INT_MAX, use long long and a strict comparison.

docs.title: Range-based for — when iterating a container
docs.text:
C++11 introduced range-based for, which iterates the elements of any container directly:

vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
for (int x : v)        cout << x << " ";   // copies each element
for (int& x : v)       x *= 2;             // modifies v
for (const int& x : v) cout << x << " ";   // reads without copying

In competitive programming, this is the cleanest way to iterate over a vector, set, map (where x is a pair<const K, V>), a string, or the adjacency list of a graph:

for (int v : adj[u]) {          // BFS/DFS neighbor iteration
    if (!visited[v]) { /* ... */ }
}

The mistake to avoid is choosing the wrong reference qualifier. This is the most common range-for bug:

for (int x : v) x *= 2;   // modifies a COPY — v is unchanged
for (int& x : v) x *= 2;  // modifies v

Use int& (or auto&) when you mean to modify. Use const int& (or const auto&) when you read a non-trivial type — a string, a vector, a large struct — because the default for (string s : vs) copies every string in the container. The performance difference in a hot loop is enormous.

Iterator invalidation. Do not modify the container's structure inside a range-based for. push_back may reallocate the underlying buffer, invalidating the implicit iterator; erase invalidates it outright:

for (int x : v) {
    if (x < 0) v.push_back(-x);   // UNDEFINED BEHAVIOR
}

If you need to modify the container during iteration, use an explicit index (for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i)) or collect the changes first and apply them after.

vector<bool> caveat. vector<bool> is a bit-packed specialization — its elements are proxies, not real bool objects. As a result, for (bool& b : vb) does not compile, and for (bool b : vb) copies a proxy that may behave unexpectedly. Use vector<char> when you need a boolean array with normal semantics; use bitset when you actually want the bit packing.

docs.title: while — when the count is unknown
docs.text:
Use while when the loop terminates based on a runtime condition, not a precomputed count. Two extremely common CP idioms:

Reading input until EOF (unknown number of test cases):

int x;
while (cin >> x) {
    // process x
}

Search until found:

int pos = -1;
int i = 0;
while (i < n && a[i] != target) ++i;
if (i < n) pos = i;

while also appears in convergence loops — fixed-point iterations, binary search, and numerical methods where the termination condition is "the update is small enough":

double lo = 0, hi = 1e9;
for (int iter = 0; iter < 100; ++iter) {     // binary search on doubles
    double mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    if (ok(mid)) lo = mid; else hi = mid;
}

(Note: in that snippet we use for with a fixed iteration count, which is the standard CP technique for binary search on double — floating-point while (hi - lo > 1e-9) can loop forever on hard inputs.)

Pitfall 1: forgetting to advance. A while loop where the condition variable is never modified runs forever. -Wall does not catch this; only reading the code catches it. When you write a while, scan the body first and confirm: does something here make the condition eventually false?

Pitfall 2: continue without advancing.

int i = 0;
while (i < n) {
    if (a[i] < 0) continue;   // BUG: i never advances — infinite loop
    cout << a[i++] << "\n";
}

The equivalent for version does not have this bug because continue still runs ++i. If you must continue in a while, advance the variable explicitly before the continue.

Pitfall 3: while (cin >> x) is false on format error, not just EOF. If input contains a non-numeric token where an int is expected, cin enters a fail state and the loop exits silently — possibly in the middle of the input, not at the end. If the problem guarantees well-formed input, this is fine. Otherwise, distinguish cin.eof() from cin.fail().

docs.title: do-while — at least once
docs.text:
The body executes first; the condition is checked afterwards. In competitive programming, do-while is rare — the "read at least one value, then repeat while not sentinel" pattern it expresses is usually clearer as a while with an explicit first read:

// do-while style:
int x;
do {
    cin >> x;
    // ...
} while (x != 0);

// equivalent, and usually clearer:
int x; cin >> x;
while (x != 0) {
    // ...
    cin >> x;
}

The one place do-while has a natural home is interactive problems with a mandatory first query, or menu-style input that always presents at least one option. For standard input-processing, prefer the while form.

Pitfall: continue in do-while jumps to the condition, not the body start. This asymmetry — for runs the update, while re-checks, do-while re-checks — is a genuine source of bugs when you convert between loop forms. If you convert a for to a do-while, re-examine every continue.

docs.title: Loop Control: break and continue
docs.text:
break exits the innermost loop. In a single loop, it is a clean early exit:

for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    if (a[i] == target) {
        cout << i << "\n";
        break;
    }
}

In nested loops, break exits only the innermost one. If you need to abandon both loops at once, three idioms:

// 1. Flag in the condition
bool found = false;
for (int i = 0; i < n && !found; ++i)
    for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j)
        if (a[i][j] == target) { found = true; break; }

// 2. goto — cleanest for this narrow case
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
    for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j)
        if (a[i][j] == target) goto done;
done:

// 3. Extract to a function and return
bool search(...) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j)
            if (a[i][j] == target) return true;
    return false;
}

In competitive programming, the flag in the condition is the most idiomatic — it keeps everything local and makes the exit condition visible at the top of the loop. The goto form is legitimate for deeply nested searches; the return form is the cleanest when the search is already inside a helper function.

break inside a switch inside a loop exits the switch, not the loop. To exit the loop from inside a switch, use return or goto:

for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    switch (a[i]) {
        case 0: break;      // exits the switch, continues the loop
        case 1: goto end;   // exits the loop (and the switch)
    }
}
end:

continue skips to the next iteration. In CP it is used mostly for filtering:

for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    if (a[i] < 0) continue;   // skip negative values
    cout << a[i] << "\n";
}

And for skipping the transition in a DP where the current state is unreachable:

for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    if (dp[i] == INF) continue;      // state never reached — skip
    dp[i + 1] = min(dp[i + 1], dp[i] + cost);
}

Both uses are fine. The only pattern to avoid is continue in a while loop without advancing the loop variable (covered above).

docs.title: Patterns You Will Reuse Constantly
docs.text:
The following idioms appear so often in competitive programming that they are worth memorizing.

Read until EOF (unknown number of test cases):

int x;
while (cin >> x) { /* process */ }

1-based indexing — many problems are stated with indices $1 \le i \le n$. Pick a convention and stick to it:

vector<int> v(n + 1);
for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) cin >> v[i];

Mixing 1-based and 0-based indexing in the same file is one of the top three sources of off-by-one bugs. If the problem uses 1-based, convert immediately at input; if it uses 0-based, keep it 0-based everywhere. Do not switch conventions halfway through.

Early-exit search — the && !found form is clearer than if (found) break:

bool found = false;
for (int i = 0; i < n && !found; ++i)
    if (a[i] == x) found = true;

Reading a grid — cin >> s reads one whitespace-delimited token, so multi-line grids parse naturally:

int n, m; cin >> n >> m;
vector<string> grid(n);
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) cin >> grid[i];

(If you use getline here, remember to flush the newline left behind by cin >> n >> m; see the I/O article.)

Iterating neighbors in a graph:

for (int v : adj[u]) {          // range-based — no iterator hassle
    if (!visited[v]) { /* ... */ }
}

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
Loops are where runtime is measured. A rough throughput table for typical contest hardware with -O2:

Loop body Approximate operations per second Empty (for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {}) $\sim 10^9$ Simple integer arithmetic $\sim 10^8 - 10^9$ Contiguous array access $\sim 10^8$ std::map / std::set operation $\sim 10^6 - 10^7$ std::unordered_map operation $\sim 10^6 - 10^7$ Random memory access (cache miss) $\sim 10^7$

These numbers are approximate but useful as a sanity check: if your solution does $10^{10}$ elementary operations, it will TLE no matter how clean your loop is. If it does $10^7$ map operations, that is already ~1 second.

What -O2 gives you automatically:

  • Loop unrolling for simple loops with a fixed small body.
  • Vectorization (SIMD) of element-wise operations on contiguous arrays — for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) c[i] = a[i] + b[i]; compiles to SSE/AVX.
  • Hoisting of loop-invariant expressions.
  • Dead-loop elimination for loops with no observable side effects.

What -O2 cannot fix:

  • The algorithm. An $O(n^2)$ solution with $n = 10^5$ is $10^{10}$ operations; no micro-optimization saves it. Get the complexity right first, then worry about the constants.
  • Cache-unfriendly memory access. Accessing a row-major 2D array column-by-column is $5$–$10\times$ slower than row-by-row because every access misses the cache:
// Slow: column-major traversal of a row-major array
for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j)
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        sum += a[i][j];

// Fast: row-major traversal (matches memory layout)
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
    for (int j = 0; j < m; ++j)
        sum += a[i][j];
  • Unnecessary allocations. vector<int> v(n) inside a hot loop is slow; declare it once outside and reuse. The same applies to string, map, and any container that allocates.

Guidance for contests. For $n \ge 10^5$, aim for $O(n \log n)$ or $O(n)$. For $n \ge 10^7$, even $O(n)$ must be tight — avoid map, avoid string concatenation in loops, prefer arrays over containers. For $n \le 10^3$, an $O(n^2)$ approach is fine; do not over-engineer.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
A checklist to run whenever your solution WAs or TLEs and you suspect control flow:

  1. if (x = 5) instead of if (x == 5) — compile with -Wall -Wextra; GCC catches this.
  2. Dangling else — use braces always.
  3. cout << cond ? a : b — wrap the ternary in parentheses when streaming.
  4. Missing break in switch — fall-through.
  5. Variable declaration in a case without braces — compile error; wrap in { ... }.
  6. for (unsigned i = n - 1; i >= 0; --i) — infinite loop; use int counters.
  7. v.size() - 1 on an empty vector — wraps to SIZE_MAX.
  8. v.size() compared to int — signed/unsigned conversion; safe only if the counter is always $\ge 0$.
  9. for (int x : v) x *= 2 — modifies a copy; use int&.
  10. for (string s : vs) — copies every string; use const string&.
  11. Modifying a container inside a range-for — iterator invalidation; use an explicit index.
  12. for (bool& b : vb) — vector<bool> is not a normal container; use vector<char>.
  13. continue in while without advancing — infinite loop.
  14. continue in do-while — jumps to the condition; re-examine conversion from for.
  15. break in nested loops — exits only the innermost; use a flag, goto, or return.
  16. break in switch inside a loop — exits the switch, not the loop.
  17. while (cin >> x) ends on format error, not just EOF — distinguish cin.eof() from cin.fail() if input may be malformed.
  18. i <= n vs i < n — the single most common source of off-by-one WA.
  19. Mixing 1-based and 0-based indices in one file — pick a convention and stick to it.
  20. for (int i = 0; i <= INT_MAX; ++i) — signed overflow is UB under -O2.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Always compile with -Wall -Wextra. Most control-flow bugs are caught by warnings before they reach the judge.
  • Always use braces around if/else bodies. The dangling-else class of bugs disappears at zero cost.
  • ++i and i++ compile to identical machine code for int under -O2. Don't optimize what doesn't matter.
  • Use signed int (or long long) for loop counters. Unsigned counters invite wrap-around infinite loops.
  • When iterating containers, const auto& avoids copies for non-trivial types; auto& modifies in place.
  • break exits only the innermost loop; use a flag, goto, or return to abandon nested loops.
  • continue in a while loop requires the loop variable to advance on the continue path; in for, it does not.
  • The algorithmic complexity dominates runtime. Get $O(n \log n)$ right before worrying about loop constants.

docs.text:
• Codeforces 1A — Theatre Square — off-by-one in ceiling division; watch for int overflow when multiplying the two dimensions.
  • Codeforces 158B — Taxi — conditionals on group sizes; a good exercise in case analysis without branching everywhere.
  • CSES — Number Spiral — nested conditionals on the parity of x and y; the canonical "if-else on structure" problem.
