docs.title: Functions and Recursion
docs.text:
Functions and recursion are two names for the same idea viewed from different angles: a function is how you factor a problem into reusable pieces, and recursion is how you let those pieces call themselves. In competitive programming, this pair is unavoidable — DFS, divide-and-conquer, segment trees, backtracking, memoized DP, and union-find with path compression are all recursive by nature. Almost every non-trivial graph algorithm you will write for the rest of this course either is a recursion or was a recursion converted to an explicit stack.

The subtlety is that recursion in CP is not the recursion of textbooks. In a contest you are under an 8 MB stack, a 1 s time limit, and a judge that compiles your code with -O2 — which changes how deep you can recurse and how much the compiler inlines. This article covers the parts that actually bite: passing parameters cheaply, understanding stack frames, memoization, and converting recursion to iteration when depth matters.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Introduction to C++ — -O2, the CP template.
  • I/O and Data Types — int vs long long, size_t, overflow.
  • Conditionals and Loops — loop idioms.
  • Arrays and Vectors — global arrays, vector, contiguous memory, iterator invalidation.

docs.title: Functions — What Actually Matters in CP
docs.text: The syntax of int f(int x) { return x + 1; } is something you already know. What follows are the parts that determine whether your solution passes or TLEs, and the parts that produce silent bugs.

docs.title: The global-state idiom
docs.text:
In CP, functions almost never receive their state through parameters. Instead, state lives in global arrays declared once at file scope, and functions read/write them directly:

constexpr int MAXN = 200'005;
vector<int> adj[MAXN];       // adjacency list
int dist[MAXN];              // BFS distances
bool visited[MAXN];          // DFS visited flags

void dfs(int u) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj[u])
        if (!visited[v]) dfs(v);
}

This is deliberately not the "clean" way to write software, but it is the CP way, for three reasons:

  1. No copying. Passing a vector<vector<int>> by value would copy the entire graph on every call. Global access is a memory read, not a copy.
  2. No stack frame bloat. Every local variable added to a recursive function's signature enlarges its stack frame, reducing the recursion depth you can afford before crashing.
  3. Contest speed. You write dfs(u), not dfs(u, adj, dist, visited, parent, ...). Fewer characters means fewer bugs under time pressure.

The one parameter that does travel through recursion is the parent — used to avoid revisiting the previous node in a tree DFS:

void dfs(int u, int p) {   // p = parent of u; 0 or -1 at the root
    for (int v : adj[u])
        if (v != p) dfs(v, u);
}

docs.title: Pass by value, reference, and const reference — the CP-relevant rules
docs.text:
void by_value(vector<int> v);            // COPIES the entire vector — usually a bug
void by_reference(vector<int>& v);       // allows modification, no copy
void by_const_ref(const vector<int>& v); // read-only, no copy — the default for input

Three practical rules:

  • Small primitives (int, long long, double, char, bool, small pair) — pass by value. Copying 8 bytes is cheaper than dereferencing a reference.
  • Containers or structs, read-only — pass by const&. This is the single most impactful habit for performance: a const vector<int>& on a $10^5$-element vector is O(1) instead of O(n) to pass.
  • Containers or structs, mutated — pass by &. Same idea, allowing writes.

The performance difference is not marginal:

long long sum_by_value(vector<int> v) {        // O(n) copy on every call
    long long s = 0;
    for (int x : v) s += x;
    return s;
}

long long sum_by_ref(const vector<int>& v) {   // O(1) pass
    long long s = 0;
    for (int x : v) s += x;
    return s;
}

For a loop that calls this $10^5$ times on vectors of size $10^5$, the first version does $10^{10}$ extra element copies — that's a TLE the compiler cannot save you from.

docs.title: Return by value — RVO makes it free
docs.text:
Returning a vector or string from a function looks expensive but usually is not. C++17 guarantees Return Value Optimization (RVO) in the common case — the return object is constructed directly in the caller's storage, with no copy and no move:

vector<int> make_range(int n) {
    vector<int> v(n);
    iota(v.begin(), v.end(), 0);
    return v;   // No copy — constructed in the caller's slot (C++17 guaranteed)
}

vector<int> v = make_range(10);

In CP, returning a pair<int, int>, tuple, or vector from a helper is idiomatic and free.

docs.title: inline — the semantic meaning, not the optimization hint
docs.text:
Most tutorials describe inline as "a hint to the compiler to insert the function body at the call site". That was true in 1995. In modern C++, inline primarily has a semantic meaning: it allows a function to be defined in a header file and included in multiple translation units without violating the One Definition Rule (ODR). The optimization hint is a legacy side effect — GCC's -O2 decides what to inline based on cost models, largely ignoring your inline keyword.

For CP, this means:

  • Don't sprinkle inline to "make your code faster". It doesn't.
  • Use inline on functions defined in headers if you ever split your code into multiple files. For single-file contest submissions, this never applies.
  • Trust -O2 to inline small functions. It does, aggressively.

Pitfall. -O2 inlines almost everything, which means your stack frames for inlineable functions disappear — useful for reducing recursion depth, but it also means your static variables inside inlined functions may behave unexpectedly if you rely on function identity. Don't use static inside recursive functions (see pitfalls below).

docs.title: Function templates — cheap generics
docs.text:
CP code often needs the same function for int and long long:

template<typename T>
T gcd(T a, T b) {
    while (b) { T t = a % b; a = b; b = t; }
    return a;
}

This is the standard CP idiom: gcd<int>(12, 18) and gcd<long long>(1e18, 1e9) compile to two independent, fully-inlined functions. __gcd from <algorithm> and std::gcd from <numeric> work too, but writing your own template is trivial and avoids namespace conflicts.

docs.title: Default arguments — a small caution
docs.text:
long long modpow(long long b, long long e, long long m = 1'000'000'007) { ... }

Convenient, but default arguments are evaluated at the call site, not at the definition, so a default that references a global constant must be visible at every call site. In single-file CP code this is fine; in multi-file builds it can produce surprises. Also, defaults only work right-to-left, so once you add one defaulted parameter, all following parameters must also be defaulted.

docs.title: Recursion — the mental model
docs.text:
A recursive function is just a function that calls itself. What makes recursion powerful in CP is that the call stack acts as an implicit data structure — it remembers the path from the root to the current state without any explicit bookkeeping in your code.

When you write:

void dfs(int u) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj[u])
        if (!visited[v]) dfs(v);
}

the compiler emits code that, on each call, pushes a frame onto the stack containing the current u and the loop iterator. When dfs(v) returns, u and the iterator are restored automatically. You get the "path from the current node to the DFS root" for free — without keeping an explicit vector of ancestors.

This is why recursion is elegant for trees, DFS, and backtracking, and awkward for simple loops. The cost is that every recursive call consumes real memory on the stack, and the depth of that stack is limited.

docs.title: Stack frames — why depth is limited
docs.text:
Each recursive call pushes a stack frame onto the call stack. The frame contains:

  • Return address (8 bytes on x86-64).
  • Saved registers (variable; often 0–48 bytes).
  • Function parameters not passed in registers.
  • Local variables (int, long long, small arrays).

Typical frame sizes for competitive C++ functions:

Function body Approximate frame size Empty function, few int locals ~32 bytes Function with 5–10 locals ~64–128 bytes Function with a local array int a[100] ~400+ bytes Function with a local vector<int> v ~24 bytes (the vector itself is on heap)

The stack limit on Linux is typically 8 MB (ulimit -s). So:

  • ~32-byte frames → depth ≈ 250,000
  • ~64-byte frames → depth ≈ 130,000
  • ~128-byte frames → depth ≈ 65,000

This is why recursion to depth $10^5$ works on most judges but not all, and why depth $10^6$ reliably segfaults.

The real numbers per judge.

  • Codeforces: submissions run in a thread with a 256 MB stack, not the default 8 MB. Depth $10^6$ typically works; depth $10^7$ is risky.
  • AtCoder: 1024 MB stack by default. Very forgiving; large recursion works.
  • CSES: 512 MB; depth $10^6$ is fine.
  • Many other judges (SPOJ, some UVa mirrors, custom judges): default 8 MB. Depth beyond ~$10^5$ crashes unpredictably.
  • Local testing on Linux: ulimit -s is typically 8192 (8 MB). See the pitfall below.

Rule of thumb: if the problem has $n \le 10^5$ and the recursion depth is bounded by $n$ (e.g., DFS on a tree), you are safe on major judges. For $n \le 10^6$, convert to iterative unless you know the judge gives a large stack.

docs.title: The setrlimit myth
docs.text:
Many CP tutorials (including the original version of this article) suggest:

#include <sys/resource.h>
void increase_stack() {
    const rlim_t kStackSize = 16 * 1024 * 1024;
    struct rlimit rl;
    int res = getrlimit(RLIMIT_STACK, &rl);
    if (res == 0 && rl.rlim_cur < kStackSize) {
        rl.rlim_cur = kStackSize;
        setrlimit(RLIMIT_STACK, &rl);
    }
}

This does not work on modern Linux. The main thread's stack is allocated by the kernel at program startup, based on the RLIMIT_STACK value at exec time. Calling setrlimit after the program has started does not enlarge the already-mapped stack — it only changes the limit for threads created afterwards. On a judge that compiles and runs your code with the default 8 MB, this function does nothing.

The reasons this code persists in tutorial-land:

  • It's a copy of a copy of a hack from 20 years ago, when the situation was different.
  • Some judges (notably Codeforces) do run submissions in a thread with a pre-set large stack size — but that is done by the judge's wrapper, not by your program calling setrlimit.
  • On old Linux kernels the main stack could still grow up to the new rlim_cur if setrlimit was called early. This is no longer reliable.

The correct advice: do not rely on setrlimit. Either (a) assume the judge gives you enough stack for the depth implied by the problem constraints, or (b) rewrite the algorithm iteratively. Do not add this function to your template.

docs.title: Converting recursion to iteration
docs.text:
When depth is a real risk, convert to an explicit stack. The transformation is mechanical:

Recursive DFS: 

void dfs(int u) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj[u])
        if (!visited[v]) dfs(v);
}

Iterative DFS, same behavior (pre-order): 

void dfs_iter(int start) {
    vector<int> stack = {start};
    while (!stack.empty()) {
        int u = stack.back();
        stack.pop_back();
        if (visited[u]) continue;
        visited[u] = true;
        for (int v : adj[u])
            if (!visited[v]) stack.push_back(v);
    }
}

The differences to be aware of:

  • Pre-order vs post-order. The iterative version processes the node when popped, which equals pre-order. If you need post-order (process node after its children), push a (u, phase) pair or push u twice — once as "to process", once as "to finish".
  • Memory. The explicit stack uses heap, not the call stack, so depth is limited only by available memory — effectively unlimited for CP.
  • Performance. Iterative DFS is typically 1.5–3× faster than recursive DFS, because there is no call/return overhead and no register saves per frame. For $10^6$-node graphs, this matters.
  • Clarity. Recursive DFS is easier to write and read for most patterns. Use iterative only when depth is a concern, or when profiling shows the recursive version is too slow.

For BFS, there is no recursive equivalent that makes sense (BFS is inherently level-by-level), so you will always write it iteratively with a queue.

docs.title: Memoization — the top-down DP pattern
docs.text:
Recursion becomes a dynamic programming technique when you cache the result of each subproblem. This is called top-down DP or memoization, and it is often the fastest way to code a DP when you are not sure which states are reachable:

constexpr int MAXN = 100'005;
long long memo[MAXN];          // 0 means "not computed" — valid only if 0 isn't a possible answer
bool computed[MAXN];           // explicit flag — the safe way

long long solve(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;
    if (computed[n]) return memo[n];
    long long result = solve(n - 1) + solve(n - 2);
    memo[n] = result;
    computed[n] = true;
    return result;
}

The sentinel choice matters:

  • 0 as sentinel works only if 0 is never a legitimate answer. Many CP solutions use this (e.g., counting paths where every count is ≥ 1).
  • -1 as sentinel works for non-negative answers, but not for signed sums that could be negative.
  • A separate bool[] works universally and costs at most one array. Use it when in doubt.

For 2D or larger state spaces, use a vector of the right dimension:

vector<vector<long long>> memo(n + 1, vector<long long>(m + 1, -1));

long long dp(int i, int j) {
    if (i == 0) return 1;
    if (memo[i][j] != -1) return memo[i][j];
    // ...
}

Pitfall. vector<vector<long long>> allocates one heap block per row — the same "row discontiguity" problem from the previous article. For DP tables accessed in nested loops, a flat vector (vector<long long> memo((n+1)*(m+1), -1) with index i*(m+1)+j) is faster and saves allocation overhead. For DP tables accessed by sparse recursion, the difference is marginal.

docs.title: Recursion + -O2 — what changes
docs.text:
At -O2, GCC performs tail-call optimization for self-recursive functions in tail position. A tail call is a recursive call that is the last operation of the function:

// Tail-recursive (TCO possible): recursive call is the last thing
long long fact_tail(int n, long long acc = 1) {
    if (n <= 1) return acc;
    return fact_tail(n - 1, acc * n);
}

// NOT tail-recursive: multiplication happens after the recursive call returns
long long fact(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;
    return n * fact(n - 1);
}

GCC at -O2 does transform tail-recursive functions into loops, eliminating the stack growth. This makes the tail-recursive version safe for arbitrarily deep recursion — but only for self-recursion. Mutual recursion (f calls g, g calls f) and non-tail recursion are not optimized.

Do not rely on TCO in CP:

  1. The transformation is not guaranteed by the C++ standard.
  2. Judges that add sanitizers or debug flags may disable it.
  3. Many functions you want to write (DFS, backtracking, merge sort) are not tail-recursive, so TCO is irrelevant.

The practical rule: if depth is a concern, write the iterative version. Relying on TCO for correctness is a source of runtime crashes that are impossible to reproduce locally.

docs.title: The std::function trap
docs.text:
When you need a recursive lambda (e.g., a one-off DFS passed to std::sort or captured in another function), the instinct is:

function<void(int)> dfs = [&](int u) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj[u])
        if (!visited[v]) dfs(v);
};
dfs(0);

This compiles and works, but has three costs:

  1. Heap allocation. std::function type-erases the lambda, which typically requires a heap allocation on construction. For a $10^6$-node graph with one DFS, the allocation is once; for nested lambdas called millions of times, it adds up.
  2. Indirection. Every call to dfs(v) goes through a virtual function pointer, adding ~5–10 ns overhead per call. On a $10^6$-call DFS, that is 5–10 ms — measurable.
  3. Inlining blocked. The compiler cannot inline a std::function call, so the body is a real function call with all the associated cost.

For one-off DFS, this is usually acceptable. For hot recursive code, use one of:

  • A global function (the standard CP choice).
  • A struct with operator() (zero-overhead, inlinable).
  • A lambda with auto using the this-trick (C++23 deducing this) or the explicit self-pass pattern:
auto dfs = [&](auto&& self, int u) -> void {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj[u])
        if (!visited[v]) self(self, v);
};
dfs(dfs, 0);

This compiles to essentially the same code as a named function — no heap allocation, no indirection, fully inlinable.

docs.title: DFS on a tree, with parent
docs.text:
void dfs(int u, int p) {
    for (int v : adj[u])
        if (v != p) {
            depth[v] = depth[u] + 1;
            dfs(v, u);
        }
}

The p (parent) parameter replaces a visited[] array for trees: since trees have no cycles, avoiding the parent is sufficient to avoid revisits. This is faster and uses one fewer array than the general graph DFS.

docs.title: DFS on a general graph
docs.text:
void dfs(int u) {
    visited[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj[u])
        if (!visited[v]) dfs(v);
}

For general graphs (with cycles), visited[] is necessary. If the graph is disconnected, call dfs(u) for every unvisited u.

docs.title: Backtracking with pruning
docs.text:
Backtracking is a DFS over a decision tree, where each node represents a partial solution and each edge a choice. The template is:

void backtrack(state, choices) {
    if (is_complete(state)) { record(state); return; }
    for (auto c : choices) {
        if (!feasible(state, c)) continue;   // pruning — the key to speed
        apply(state, c);
        backtrack(state, next_choices);
        undo(state, c);                       // restore state — the "backtrack"
    }
}

The canonical example is N-Queens:

int n;
vector<int> queens(n);       // queens[r] = column of the queen in row r
int solutions = 0;

bool can_place(int r, int c) {
    for (int prev_r = 0; prev_r < r; ++prev_r) {
        int prev_c = queens[prev_r];
        if (prev_c == c) return false;                    // same column
        if (abs(prev_c - c) == r - prev_r) return false;  // same diagonal
    }
    return true;
}

void solve(int r) {
    if (r == n) { ++solutions; return; }
    for (int c = 0; c < n; ++c) {
        if (!can_place(r, c)) continue;   // prune — only try feasible columns
        queens[r] = c;
        solve(r + 1);
    }
}

Two observations that matter more than the template itself:

  1. Pruning is everything. Without the if (!can_place(...)) check, N-Queens would explore $n^n$ possibilities. With pruning, $n = 8$ explores only 92 solutions, and $n = 12$ is fast.
  2. undo is the source of bugs. Every apply must have a matching undo before the recursion returns. Missing it produces nonsense results that are painful to debug. The "push/backtrack with pop_back" pattern in the original subset example is the simplest case: current.push_back(x) must always be followed by current.pop_back() after the recursive call.

docs.title: Recursive segment tree
docs.text:
Segment trees are naturally recursive: a tree node represents a range [l, r], and the children represent [l, m] and [m+1, r].

constexpr int MAXN = 100'005;
long long tree[4 * MAXN];
long long a[MAXN];

void build(int node, int l, int r) {
    if (l == r) { tree[node] = a[l]; return; }
    int m = (l + r) / 2;
    build(2 * node, l, m);
    build(2 * node + 1, m + 1, r);
    tree[node] = tree[2 * node] + tree[2 * node + 1];
}

long long query(int node, int l, int r, int ql, int qr) {
    if (qr < l || r < ql) return 0;              // disjoint
    if (ql <= l && r <= qr) return tree[node];   // fully covered
    int m = (l + r) / 2;
    return query(2 * node, l, m, ql, qr)
         + query(2 * node + 1, m + 1, r, ql, qr);
}

The recursion depth is $O(\log n)$, so no stack concerns — a segment tree on $10^6$ elements has depth ~20. This is one of the cases where recursion is always the right choice: the iterative version is a mess of bit manipulation and barely faster.

docs.title: Recursive union-find with path compression
docs.text:
int parent[MAXN], sz[MAXN];

int find(int x) {
    if (parent[x] == x) return x;
    return parent[x] = find(parent[x]);   // path compression
}

The parent[x] = find(parent[x]) line is the path compression: it flattens the tree by making every node point directly to its root. The resulting amortized cost is nearly $O(1)$ per query, and the recursion depth is bounded by the rank (logarithmic before compression, $\le \log n$ after). This is safe — depth never exceeds 20 for $n = 10^6$.

The iterative version is slightly faster:

int find(int x) {
    while (parent[x] != x) {
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];   // path halving
        x = parent[x];
    }
    return x;
}

For most CP code, the recursive version is fine — the depth bound guarantees no overflow.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
Operation Typical cost Function call, small body, inlined (-O2) 0 (absorbed into caller) Function call, non-inlined ~2–5 ns Recursive call, ~64-byte frame ~5–10 ns + stack pointer adjustment Recursive call via std::function ~10–15 ns + heap lookup Memoized recursive DP (hit) ~5 ns for the array lookup Memoized recursive DP (miss) ~100 ns + the work of the subproblem Iterative DFS (vs recursive) 1.5–3× faster

When recursion is the right choice:

  • Depth is small or bounded by $O(\log n)$ (segment trees, DSU with path compression, divide-and-conquer on arrays).
  • The problem is naturally recursive (DFS on trees, backtracking).
  • You are prototyping and clarity matters more than 30% speed.

When recursion is the wrong choice:

  • Depth could approach $10^5$ or $10^6$ and the judge may have a small stack (SPOJ, some UVa).
  • The recursive call is on the hot path (inner loop of a $10^7$-iteration computation).
  • You are writing BFS or any algorithm that is inherently iterative.

When it does not matter:

  • Memoized DP where the number of states is small but the transitions are cheap. The recursion depth is bounded by the state dimension, usually small.
  • Segment trees, DSU, and other $O(\log n)$-depth structures.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
Checklist for when a solution with functions or recursion WAs, TLEs, or crashes:

  1. Missing base case — infinite recursion → stack overflow (segfault, or silent crash on some judges).
  2. int overflow in recursive factorial — 21! overflows long long. Compute factorials modulo a prime, or use __int128, or use big-int emulation.
  3. Naive recursive Fibonacci — $O(\phi^n)$ calls, impractical for $n > 40$. Use iterative $O(n)$ or matrix exponentiation $O(\log n)$.
  4. setrlimit doesn't increase the main thread stack — modern Linux ignores it after startup. Don't rely on it.
  5. Default stack is 8 MB — a 100,000-deep recursion with 64-byte frames uses ~6 MB; a 1,000,000-deep recursion segfaults.
  6. Passing a container by value — O(n) copy per call; use const&.
  7. std::function for hot recursion — heap allocation + indirection; use a global function or self-pass lambda.
  8. Missing undo in backtracking — a push_back without a matching pop_back produces garbage.
  9. static variables inside recursive functions — the static is shared across all recursion levels, not per-frame. This is almost never what you want.
  10. vector<bool> in a visited array — proxy references; use vector<char> or global bool[].
  11. Recursion depth in a tree chain — a path graph of $10^5$ nodes is depth $10^5$; on judges with 8 MB stacks, this crashes. Convert to iterative DFS.
  12. Modifying a container inside recursive iteration — invalidation; same as the loop pitfall from the previous article.
  13. Missing parent parameter in tree DFS — you revisit the parent endlessly if the graph is a tree and you have no visited[] guard.
  14. visited set after the recursive call instead of before — leads to revisiting the node during recursion, producing cycles or exponential blowup.
  15. Recursive segment tree on $n = 0$ — build(1, 0, -1) recurses forever; guard with if (n == 0) return;.
  16. Memoization with -1 sentinel when -1 is a valid answer — false "already computed" hits. Use a bool flag array.
  17. Overlapping state in memoization — memoizing on the wrong key (e.g., memoizing solve(i) when the state is actually (i, j)) produces wrong answers silently.
  18. Recursive sort comparator — the comparator must be a strict weak ordering; do not call sort recursively inside a comparator.
  19. Tail-recursive Fibonacci — the transformation requires an accumulator; naive fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) is not tail-recursive and gets no TCO.
  20. Assuming inline makes code faster — GCC's -O2 decides; the keyword is a semantic tool, not a performance tool.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Functions in CP read state from global arrays, not parameters. Pass only the parent (tree DFS) or small indices.
  • Always pass containers by const& unless you intend to modify them. The performance difference is not marginal.
  • Return by value is free thanks to RVO; returning a vector from a helper costs nothing.
  • inline is a semantic keyword (ODR), not a performance hint. Trust -O2 to inline small functions.
  • Each recursive call uses a real stack frame (~32–128 bytes) on an 8 MB default stack. Depth above ~$10^5$ is risky on judges without large stacks.
  • Codeforces gives 256 MB stack; AtCoder ~1 GB; many smaller judges give the default 8 MB. Assume 8 MB unless you know otherwise.
  • setrlimit does not enlarge the main thread stack on modern Linux. Do not rely on it. Convert to iterative when depth matters.
  • Memoization turns recursion into top-down DP. Choose the sentinel (0, -1, or explicit bool[]) based on the answer range.
  • Recursion is always right for segment trees, DSU, and divide-and-conquer with $O(\log n)$ depth. It is usually right for DFS and backtracking. It is almost never right for depth $10^6$ without an explicit stack.
  • Backtracking = recursion + apply + undo. Every push_back must have its pop_back.

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text:
• CSES — Building Roads — connected components via DFS; test the recursive version against an iterative one on a chain input.
  • CSES — Subordinates — tree DP via recursion; small depth, ideal for learning the pattern.
  • CSES — Tree Diameter — two DFS passes; recursion depth equals the longest path — test both forms.
  • Codeforces 4C — Registration System — not recursion, but good practice with map lookups inside loops that resemble recursion.
  • CSES — N-Queens — classic backtracking with pruning; the canonical DFS-with-undo problem.
  • Codeforces 1526C1 — Potions (Easy) — iteratively re-derives a greedy result; a good contrast with the recursive DP formulation.
  • CSES — Company Queries I — binary lifting on trees; the classic case where an $O(\log n)$ recursive formulation is replaced with an iterative doubling table.

Before starting this course, you should be comfortable with:

docs.title: What is C++?
docs.text: C++ is a general-purpose, compiled, statically-typed language created by Bjarne Stroustrup as an extension of C. It supports procedural, object-oriented, and generic paradigms, and is standardized by ISO. The standards relevant for competitive programming are C++17 (widely supported) and C++20 (supported on modern judges). Anything older than C++17 is best avoided today.

docs.title: Why C++ for Competitive Programming?
docs.text:
Competitive programming requires solving algorithmic problems under strict time and memory limits. C++ dominates for several reasons:

  • Execution speed. As a compiled language, C++ produces highly optimized native code. In practice, equivalent $O(n \log n)$ solutions in C++ often run 10–50× faster than in Python, and 1.5–3× faster than in Java. On many problems with tight limits, C++ passes where Python is guaranteed to TLE.
  • Memory efficiency. Fine-grained control over allocation and object layout. Problems routinely cap memory at 256 MB or 512 MB; STL containers have far smaller overhead than Python's.
  • Standard Template Library (STL). Efficient containers (vector, set, map, unordered_map, priority_queue) and algorithms (sort, lower_bound, next_permutation, etc.) drastically reduce implementation time.
  • Universal judge support. Every major judge (Codeforces, AtCoder, CSES, CodeChef, SPOJ, UVa, TopCoder) supports GCC with modern standards and -O2.
  • Low-level and high-level features. Readable high-level code, with hand-optimization reserved for the critical 5%.

docs.title: Comparison with other languages
docs.text:
Language Speed vs C++ STL equivalent Role in CP C++ 1× (reference) Rich (STL) Dominant Java ~2–3× slower java.util.* Second most popular Python ~20–50× slower Built-in, slow Prototyping, easy problems Rust ~1–1.5× Moderate Growing, less common

Rule of thumb. If a problem expects an $O(n \log n)$ C++ solution in 1 s at $n = 2 \cdot 10^5$, an $O(n \log n)$ Python solution will often take 5–10 s and TLE. Language choice matters.

docs.title: Setting Up a C++ Environment
docs.text: The reference compiler is GCC (g++). Almost every judge uses it, so always test locally with g++. Clang works too but differs in warnings and in how it treats some undefined behavior.

docs.title: Recommended compiler flags
docs.text:
For submission (what judges effectively do):

g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o program program.cpp

For debugging locally (never submit these binaries):

g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG -o program program.cpp
  • -std=c++17 — Enable C++17. Most judges support it; some support C++20. Don't rely on C++20 features unless the judge explicitly advertises them.
  • -O2 — Optimization. This approximates what judges use. Always test with -O2: undefined behavior (out-of-bounds stack access, signed overflow) can behave differently under optimization, and performance changes dramatically.
  • -Wall -Wextra — Warnings. Take them seriously; they catch real bugs.
  • -g — Debug symbols. Required for sanitizers to produce useful traces.
  • -fsanitize=address,undefined — Runtime detection of memory errors and undefined behavior. ~2–10× slower; use only while debugging.
  • -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG — Turns some silent STL bugs (e.g., out-of-bounds vector::operator[]) into runtime errors. Also slow.

Pitfall. Debug builds can hide or expose bugs that the judge build does not. Always time your solution with the exact submission flags.

docs.title: Which standard header to include?
docs.text:
Two viable styles:

  1. Explicit includes — #include <vector>, #include <iostream>, … Portable, slower to write.
  2. #include <bits/stdc++.h> — GCC-specific umbrella header that pulls in nearly the whole standard library. Ubiquitous in competitive programming and supported on virtually every judge. Use it for contests; avoid it in production code.

For the rest of this course we use <bits/stdc++.h> for brevity.

docs.title: The Competitive Programming Template
docs.text:
Almost every solution starts from a fixed template. Memorize it.

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

using ll  = long long;
using ull = unsigned long long;
using pii = pair<int, int>;
using vi  = vector<int>;

int main() {
    ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    // solution goes here
    return 0;
}

Two lines are essential for I/O performance and are explained in the next article:

  • ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false); — Unsynchronizes C and C++ I/O streams.
  • cin.tie(nullptr); — Prevents cin from flushing cout before each read.

Do not mix C-style (scanf/printf) and C++-style (cin/cout) I/O after calling sync_with_stdio(false); doing so is undefined behavior.

docs.title: Your First Program
docs.text:
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    cout << "Welcome to the C++ course for Competitive Programming!\n";
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
1. #include <iostream> — Provides cin and cout. In real solutions we use <bits/stdc++.h> instead.
  2. using namespace std; — Brings std:: into scope. Convenient in CP; discouraged in large codebases because it pollutes the namespace. It is standard practice on judges.
  3. int main() { ... } — Program entry point.
  4. cout << ... << "\n"; — Writes to standard output. Prefer "\n" over endl; see the pitfall section.
  5. return 0; — Success exit code.

docs.title: Compiling and Running
docs.text:
Assuming the file is program.cpp:

g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -o program program.cpp
./program

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text: These trip up beginners constantly. Each one is worth memorizing.

docs.title: 1. endl vs "\n"
docs.text: endl inserts a newline and flushes the stream. Flushing on every line is catastrophic on output-heavy problems — a solution that would otherwise pass can TLE by a factor of 5–10×. Always use " ". cout << ' ' is even marginally faster than " " since it's a character, not a C-string.

docs.title: 2. Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior
docs.text:
int a = 1'000'000'000, b = 1'000'000'000;
int c = a + b;   // UB; with -O2 the compiler may assume this never happens

Use long long (ll) when the product of two ints can exceed $2^{31}-1 \approx 2.15 \cdot 10^9$, and cast at least one operand:

ll c = 1LL * a * b;   // correct

For values beyond $2^{63}-1$, use __int128 (GCC-only) or big-integer emulation.

docs.title: 3. Mixing cin/cout with scanf/printf
docs.text: After ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false), using both families is undefined behavior. Pick one — either is fine as long as you're consistent.

docs.title: 4. Recursion depth
docs.text:
The default stack is typically 8 MB. Recursive functions with deep recursion (e.g., DFS on a path of length $10^6$) overflow it and crash — often as a stack overflow, sometimes as a wrong answer under -O2. Remedies:

  • Increase the stack in your shell: ulimit -s unlimited (local only).
  • Allocate large arrays globally (static storage), not on the stack.
  • Convert deep recursion to an explicit stack or iterative DP.

docs.title: 5. vector::operator[] does not bounds-check
docs.text: v[i] with i >= v.size() is undefined behavior. Only use v.at(i) when you want a runtime error (e.g., during debugging). Similarly, array[n] on a fixed-size array is UB.

docs.title: Debugging Locally
docs.text: Two habits that save enormous time:

docs.title: Print macro
docs.text:
#define dbg(x) cerr << #x << " = " << (x) << '\n'

cerr is not tied to cout, so it won't interleave awkwardly, and you can disable it before submission with a single #define.

docs.title: Sanitizers and stress testing
docs.text: Compile with -fsanitize=address,undefined to catch memory errors and UB during practice. Combine with stress testing (generate random small inputs, compare against a brute force) to catch logical bugs before the judge does. Stress testing is covered later in this course.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• C++ is the dominant CP language thanks to speed and STL. Always compile with -O2 when timing.
  • Use <bits/stdc++.h> and the standard template.
  • "\n" over endl; unbuffer cin/cout; never mix C and C++ I/O after sync_with_stdio(false).
  • Beware signed integer overflow, shallow stack depth, and vector::operator[] without bounds checks.
  • Debug with sanitizers; submit with the judge's flags.

docs.text:

  • Comfort with the terminal to compile and run programs.

This article is the second in the course. It assumes the standard CP template from the previous article:

#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    // ...
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Fast I/O for Competitive Programming
docs.text:
The default cin/cout is synchronized with C's stdio (scanf/printf) so that both families can be freely mixed. This synchronization runs on every I/O operation and is a measurable bottleneck when input or output is large (commonly $10^5$–$10^6$ numbers in CP).

Two calls disable it:

ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);
cin.tie(nullptr);

docs.title: What each one does
docs.text:
• sync_with_stdio(false) — Removes the synchronization layer. After this, cin reads directly from the C++ stream buffer without checking that stdio is consistent, making reads significantly faster (often 3–5×).
  • cin.tie(nullptr) — By default cin is tied to cout, meaning cout is flushed before every cin read. On a program that interleaves reads and writes, this causes gratuitous flushes. Untying removes them.

docs.title: The critical pitfall: do not mix families
docs.text:
After sync_with_stdio(false):

ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);
cout << "hello\n";
printf("world\n");   // UNDEFINED BEHAVIOR

Output order between cout and printf is no longer guaranteed. If you disable sync, use only cin/cout, or only scanf/printf, for the rest of the program.

Similarly, cin.tie(nullptr) means you must call cout.flush() explicitly if you need flushing — critical for interactive problems. Interactive problems require flushing after each query:

cout << "? " << x << "\n";
cout.flush();                    // mandatory in interactive mode
int response; cin >> response;

docs.title: endl vs "\n" vs '\n'
docs.text:
Expression Type written Flush endl char + flush() Yes — avoid " " const char* (calls strlen) No ' ' char No — marginal speedup

On output-heavy problems (e.g., $10^6$ lines), endl can cause 5–10× slowdown and guaranteed TLE. Use ' '. Use endl only when you intend to flush (i.e., interactive problems or before crashing).

docs.title: When cin with fast I/O is still not enough
docs.text:
For extremely tight limits (e.g., $10^7$ integers), a custom fread-based reader is 2–4× faster than cin even with sync disabled. It's rarely needed on modern judges but worth knowing:

namespace io {
    constexpr int BUF = 1 << 16;
    static char buf[BUF];
    static int pos = 0, len = 0;
    inline char rc() {
        if (pos == len) { len = fread(buf, 1, BUF, stdin); pos = 0; if (len <= 0) return 0; }
        return buf[pos++];
    }
    template<typename T> inline bool readInt(T &out) {
        char c; T sign = 1, num = 0;
        if (!(c = rc())) return false;
        while (c < '0' || c > '9') { if (c == '-') { sign = -1; c = rc(); break; } if (!(c = rc())) return false; }
        for (; c >= '0' && c <= '9'; c = rc()) num = num * 10 + (c - '0');
        out = sign * num;
        return true;
    }
}

Warning. Mixing this with cin/cout is undefined behavior. Use it only in programs that read exclusively through io::rc and write through printf or a similar raw output.

docs.title: How cin >> parses
docs.text:
cin >> x skips leading whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) and reads until the next whitespace. This means:

int a, b; cin >> a >> b;
// input "   3

    42   " works identically to "3 42"
  • Multi-line input does not require any special handling — cin >> treats as whitespace.
  • For strings, cin >> s reads up to the next whitespace. To read a whole line with spaces, use getline.

docs.title: Reading until EOF
docs.text:
A common judge format: read an unknown number of values until the end of the input.

int x;
while (cin >> x) {
    // process x
}

cin >> x evaluates to the stream itself, which converts to false if the stream is in a fail state (EOF or a format error). Equivalent with scanf:

while (scanf("%d", &x) == 1) { /* ... */ }

scanf returns the number of items successfully assigned, so == 1 (or != EOF) is the idiomatic check.

docs.title: Reading a whole line
docs.text:
string s;
getline(cin, s);   // reads up to and including '\n', discards the '\n'

Classic pitfall. cin >> leaves the trailing newline in the buffer. A subsequent getline reads an empty string and returns immediately:

int n; cin >> n;
string s;
getline(cin, s);       // BUG: reads empty string (the leftover '\n')

Fixes:

cin.ignore(numeric_limits<streamsize>::max(), '\n');
getline(cin, s);

or, more idiomatically:

cin >> ws;             // skip all leading whitespace, including '\n'
getline(cin, s);

docs.title: Reading characters
docs.text:
char c;
c = getchar();         // fast; from <cstdio>
c = cin.get();         // slow; from <iostream>

For single-character input in tight loops (grid problems), getchar() (or getchar_unlocked() on GCC) is the fastest option.

docs.title: Chaining
docs.text:
cout << "Sum: " << a + b << "
";

<< returns the stream, so it chains naturally. ' ' (a char) is marginally faster than " " (a C-string) because the char overload doesn't call strlen.

docs.title: Formatting floating point
docs.text:
By default, cout may print doubles in scientific notation (e.g., 1e+06), which is a frequent WA cause. Force fixed-point with fixed and set precision:

double ans = 0.1 + 0.2;
cout << fixed << setprecision(10) << ans << "\n";  // 0.3000000000

fixed and setprecision are sticky — they affect all subsequent writes to cout until reset (cout << defaultfloat;).

Alternatively, use printf:

printf("%.10f\n", ans);

But only if you never called sync_with_stdio(false) and use printf for all output.

docs.title: Large integers stored in double
docs.text:
double x = 123456789012345;
cout << x << "\n";   // 1.23456789012345e+14 — scientific notation!

This is another reason to use fixed. But note: double can exactly represent integers only up to $2^{53} \approx 9 \cdot 10^{15}$. Beyond that, precision is silently lost. Never use double to store large integer counts.

docs.title: Data Types
docs.text: Choosing the right type is the single most common source of silent wrong answers. Overflow, truncation, and sign errors rarely crash — they just produce plausible-looking wrong values.

docs.title: Integer types — what's guaranteed vs what's typical
docs.text:
The C++ standard only guarantees minimum ranges. On all modern judges (g++ on Linux x86-64):

Type Guaranteed minimum On judges Range on judges short 16 bits 16 bits $[-2^{15}, 2^{15}-1]$ int 16 bits 32 bits $[-2^{31}, 2^{31}-1] \approx [-2.1\cdot10^9, 2.1\cdot10^9]$ long 32 bits 64 bits on Linux, 32 on Windows — (avoid) long long 64 bits 64 bits $[-2^{63}, 2^{63}-1] \approx [-9.2\cdot10^{18}, 9.2\cdot10^{18}]$ size_t — 64 bits unsigned $[0, 2^{64}-1]$

Portability pitfall. long is 32-bit on Windows and 64-bit on Linux. Judges run Linux, so long behaves like long long there, but a solution developed on Windows with long will behave differently. Never use long in competitive code — use int or long long.

docs.title: Fixed-width types
docs.text:
For maximum portability and explicit width, use <cstdint>:

int32_t x;       // always 32-bit signed
int64_t y;       // always 64-bit signed
uint32_t z;      // always 32-bit unsigned

CP code often prefers using ll = long long; for brevity.

docs.title: Signed overflow is undefined behavior
docs.text:
int a = 1'000'000'000;
int b = a + a;    // UB — signed overflow

With -O2, the compiler is allowed to assume this never happens, and may produce code that misbehaves in ways you cannot debug from the source:

if (a + b < 0) { /* compiler may eliminate this branch entirely */ }

There are two correct options:

  1. Use long long whenever a sum or product of ints can exceed $2.1 \cdot 10^9$.
  2. Use unsigned if you accept the modular wrap-around semantics (see below) — rarely the right choice in CP.
int a = 1'000'000'000, b = 1'000'000'000;
long long c = (long long)a * b;    // correct; promotes before multiply
long long d = 1LL * a * b;         // idiomatic short form

docs.title: Unsigned types — wrap-around and mixed comparison
docs.text:
unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo $2^N$ — no UB, but often not what you want:

unsigned int x = 0;
cout << (x - 1);    // 4294967295, not -1

Worse, comparisons between signed and unsigned convert the signed operand to unsigned:

int n = -1;
vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3};
if (n < v.size()) { /* FALSE! n is converted to a huge unsigned value */ }

This is the source of countless real bugs. Practical rule: avoid unsigned in CP, except for bitmask tricks and hash computations where wrap-around is desired.

docs.title: size_t — the .size() return type
docs.text:
All STL .size() methods return size_t (unsigned). Direct comparisons with int are the canonical trigger of the pitfall above. Two safe idioms:

vector<int> v;
for (int i = 0; i < (int)v.size(); i++) { ... }       // explicit cast
for (size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); i++) { ... }         // use size_t throughout

And never write:

for (int i = 0; i <= (int)v.size() - 1; i++) { ... }  // BUG: infinite loop if v is empty

because (int)0 - 1 = -1, then -1 <= huge is false only by luck; with size_t, 0 - 1 = SIZE_MAX → infinite loop.

docs.title: __int128 — beyond 64 bits
docs.text:
GCC provides a 128-bit integer for values exceeding long long (e.g., multiplying two $10^{18}$ values, or RSA-like problems):

__int128 x = (__int128)a * b;   // a, b are long long

There is no cin >> overload for __int128. Read and print manually:

// read
long long hi, lo;   // hi * 2^64 + lo ... custom parsing
// print
void print128(__int128 x) {
    if (x == 0) { cout << '0'; return; }
    if (x < 0) { cout << '-'; x = -x; }
    string s;
    while (x > 0) { s += char('0' + x % 10); x /= 10; }
    reverse(s.begin(), s.end());
    cout << s;
}

Non-portable (GCC/Clang only; not on MSVC), but every judge uses GCC.

docs.title: Floating point types
char — signedness is implementation-defined
docs.text:
Whether plain char is signed or unsigned is implementation-defined. On x86-64 Linux judges, char is signed, meaning char c = 200; actually stores -56. This matters when:

  • Passing char to <cctype> functions:
char c = ...;
if (isalpha(c)) { ... }               // UB if c is negative!
if (isalpha((unsigned char)c)) { ... } // correct
  • Indexing with character values as integers: int idx = c - 'a'; is fine because ASCII ranges are contiguous, but c - '0' combined with isdigit has the same signedness trap.

docs.title: bool
docs.text: bool is 1 byte on virtually all platforms. vector<bool> is a specialization packed into bits — its elements are not real bool& references, &v[i] does not compile, and concurrent modification of adjacent elements is data-race-prone. Use vector<char> or bitset when you need an array of booleans with normal semantics.

docs.title: Implicit conversions
docs.text:
C++ converts types silently. Most are harmless, but narrowing (large → small) truncates:

long long x = 3'000'000'000;
int y = x;              // implementation-defined (wraps to a negative number on GCC)

Curly-brace initialization rejects narrowing at compile time:

int a{1'000'000'000};   // OK
int b{3'000'000'000};   // compile error: narrowing — good, catches the bug early

Use {} initialization for constants; it turns silent bugs into compile errors.

docs.title: Multiplication overflow before casting
docs.text:
int a = 1'000'000'000, b = 1'000'000'000;
long long c = (long long)a * b;   // CORRECT: cast before multiply
long long d = (long long)(a * b); // WRONG: overflow happens as int first

The rule: cast one operand before the operation, not the result.

docs.title: static_cast vs C-style cast
docs.text:
Prefer static_cast<T>(x) in modern code:

int a = static_cast<int>(some_double);

C-style (int) still works but is more permissive and harder to search for. In competitive code, either is acceptable; in learning code, use static_cast.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
Common idioms for the "infinity" value used in shortest paths, DP initialization, etc.:

const int INF      = 1'000'000'000;               // fits in int
const long long LINF = 1'000'000'000'000'000'000LL; // fits in ll
const int MOD      = 1'000'000'007;               // prime, common in problems

Pitfall. Adding two INFs overflows an int: INF + INF = 2e9 fits, but INF + INF + INF overflows. Common trick: initialize with INF / 2 or INF / 3 so that 2 * INF and INF + x never overflow. Alternatively, use LINF for all DP values and let the compiler's 64-bit arithmetic absorb the sum.

For compile-time constants, prefer constexpr (C++11+) over const:

constexpr int MAX_N = 200'005;
constexpr int MOD   = 1'000'000'007;

constexpr guarantees the value is computed at compile time. const only guarantees "not modified".

docs.title: Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
A checklist to review whenever a solution gets WA or TLE:

  1. endl instead of '\n' — the #1 cause of TLE on output-heavy problems.
  2. ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false) without cin.tie(nullptr) — half the speedup lost.
  3. Mixing printf/scanf with cin/cout after disabling sync — undefined behavior, garbled output.
  4. int overflow — sums of $10^9 + 10^9$, products of $10^5 \cdot 10^5$, factorials above $12!$, etc. Use long long.
  5. (long long)(a * b) instead of (long long)a * b — the multiplication overflows before the cast.
  6. unsigned comparison — int n = -1; n < v.size() is false.
  7. v.size() - 1 on an empty vector — wraps to SIZE_MAX.
  8. getline after cin >> — reads the leftover newline; use cin >> ws.
  9. Double == comparison — always use epsilon.
  10. Printing doubles without fixed — scientific notation causes WA.
  11. Storing long long counts in double — silent precision loss above $2^{53}$.
  12. isalpha(c) with negative char — cast to unsigned char first.
  13. vector<bool> misuse — not a normal container; &v[i] fails.
  14. long on Windows vs Linux — use long long for 64-bit values.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Always include ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr); and use '\n', never endl.
  • After disabling sync, use either cin/cout or scanf/printf — never both.
  • Use long long for any value that can exceed $2.1 \cdot 10^9$; cast before multiplying.
  • Never compare doubles with ==; use abs(a - b) < EPS.
  • Never use unsigned or long in competitive code; use int, long long, and size_t (only for .size()).
  • Use constexpr for constants; INF = 1e9, LINF = 1e18, and be careful summing them.
  • Watch for getline after cin >>; use cin >> ws to skip leftover newlines.
  • Format doubles with fixed << setprecision(10) or printf("%.10f").

docs.title: Practice and Problems
docs.text:
Every other article in this course teaches a technique. This one teaches how to learn the techniques — the meta-skill that determines whether you spend six months going in circles or six months building a rating that reflects your actual ability. Competitive programming is unusual in that the raw material (problems, editorials, judges) is completely free and unlimited, yet most people who start never reach their potential. The reason is almost never intelligence. It is that they practice the wrong way: they solve problems without reflecting, look at editorials too early, avoid the discomfort of contest mode, and never target their specific weaknesses. This article is about avoiding those failure modes.

The roadmap below is not a schedule — it is a set of mastery criteria with concrete problem lists and debugging techniques behind each. Move through the phases as fast as you can honestly demonstrate the criteria, not on a calendar.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The other articles in this course through Algorithmic Complexity — you cannot practice what you have not learned.
  • A working C++ environment with g++, -O2, and the CP template.
  • Accounts on Codeforces and CSES.

docs.title: The Two Modes of Practice
docs.text: Almost all effective practice falls into one of two categories, and confusing them is the most common reason for stalled progress.

docs.title: Topic-focused practice
docs.text:
You pick one technique (prefix sums, binary search on the answer, monotonic stack) and solve 5–10 problems where it is the intended solution. The goal is depth: by the end, you should be able to implement the technique from memory in 5 minutes, recognize when it applies, and know its standard variations.

Where this practice lives:

  • CSES Problem Set — the gold standard for topic-focused practice. Each section (Sorting and Searching, Dynamic Programming, Graph Algorithms) contains 20–30 problems sorted roughly by difficulty, all solvable with the section's technique. If you only use one resource, use this.
  • USACO Guide — organized by topic with a difficulty rating per problem (Very Easy / Easy / Normal / Hard / Very Hard) that is more calibrated than raw problem ratings.
  • Codeforces EDU — structured courses on specific techniques, with a mix of theory and practice.
  • CP-Algorithms — this site; each algorithm article has a "Practice Problems" section at the bottom.

The signature of good topic-focused practice: you can feel the technique becoming reflexive. When you read a problem and think "this smells like prefix sums" before consciously reasoning, the technique has moved from working memory to long-term memory. That is the goal.

docs.title: Contest-mode practice
docs.text:
You sit down for 90 minutes to 2 hours, read 5–8 mixed problems of unknown technique, and try to solve as many as you can under time pressure. The goal is speed and judgment: reading comprehension, problem classification, code implementation under stress, and — most importantly — knowing when to abandon a problem.

Where this practice lives:

  • Codeforces contests — Div. 3 and Div. 4 weekly, Div. 2 twice a month, Div. 1 monthly. Rated and unrated.
  • AtCoder Beginner Contests (ABC) — every Saturday, well-designed problems with an accessible difficulty curve.
  • Virtual contests — Codeforces lets you replay any past contest as if it were live, with the original 2-hour timer. This is the single most underrated practice technique in CP.

The signature of good contest-mode practice: your rating rises (or at least your solve rate on problems at or below your level rises). The feedback is immediate and honest. You cannot fake it.

docs.title: Why you need both
docs.text: Topic-focused practice without contests produces a contestant who can solve a specific technique on request but freezes on a mixed set. Contest-mode practice without topic-focus produces a contestant who can solve easy problems quickly but never learns the techniques that unlock hard problems. Both, interleaved, is the only path that works. A common ratio is 70% topic-focused during the week, 30% contests on weekends.

docs.title: The Four Phases: Mastery Criteria, Not Timeboxes
docs.text: The original roadmap suggested "1–4 weeks" per phase. That advice is almost always wrong, because the phase duration depends entirely on prior programming background: a computer-science student can clear Phase 1 in a week; a total beginner may need three months. The right structure is a set of mastery criteria you can honestly test yourself against.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Fundamentals
docs.text:
Mastery criteria (all must be true):

  • You can solve any problem in CSES "Introductory Problems" in under 15 minutes, with zero WAs on the first submission. There are 22 problems in that section; if you can go through them in a week with no failed submissions, you have mastered Phase 1.
  • You can implement a loop with for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) without thinking, and you never make off-by-one errors at boundaries (i < n vs i <= n, empty input, n = 1).
  • You know that 10^5 is not 100000 and never write it in code.
  • You can read 300 words of problem statement and correctly identify the input format, output format, and edge cases.

Typical time to mastery: 1–2 weeks for someone with prior programming experience, 6–12 weeks for a true beginner. Do not rush; the cost of shaky fundamentals is a permanent ceiling of ~1200 Codeforces.

Problems (each teaches a specific reflex):

Problem Teaches CSES — Weird Algorithm Simulation, the while (n != 1) loop CSES — Missing Number Sum of arithmetic sequence, reading large inputs efficiently CSES — Repetitions Sequential scan, running counter CSES — Increasing Array Greedy from left to right, overflow CSES — Permutations Constructive thinking, the case-analysis discipline CSES — Two Sets Parity reasoning, sum divisibility, overflow in sums of 10^5 elements Codeforces 4A — Watermelon Reading comprehension, edge cases (w = 2 cannot be split) Codeforces 71A — Way Too Long Words String handling, s.front() / s.back() Codeforces 231A — Team Counting with a condition

docs.title: Phase 2 — Arrays, Sorting, and Searching
docs.text:
Mastery criteria:

  • You can solve any problem in CSES "Sorting and Searching" in under 30 minutes.
  • You can implement sort with a custom comparator, lower_bound, upper_bound, and the sort + unique + erase deduplication without looking them up.
  • You can convert a problem statement into a sorted array + binary search or prefix sums + range query in your head before writing code.
  • You have solved at least 3 Codeforces Div. 2 A or B problems with 0 WAs on first submission.

Typical time: 2–4 weeks.

Problems:

Problem Teaches CSES — Distinct Numbers sort + unique + erase, and the "count distinct" reflex CSES — Apartments Two-pointer on two sorted arrays CSES — Ferris Wheel Greedy with two pointers CSES — Concert Tickets multiset with upper_bound + erase(iterator) — the classic multiset pitfall CSES — Maximum Subarray Sum Kadane's algorithm; the difference between $O(n^2)$ naive and $O(n)$ solution CSES — Two Sum Not LeetCode's Two Sum — this is pair-sum: sort + two pointers, or map lookup CSES — Playlist Sliding window + map, longest substring without repeating Codeforces 339B — Xenia and Ringroad Simulation with modular arithmetic, off-by-one Codeforces 580A — Kefa and First Steps Longest increasing consecutive segment

docs.title: Phase 3 — STL and Data Structures
docs.text:
Mastery criteria:

  • You can solve any problem in CSES "Data Structures" (the 20-ish problems there) in under 45 minutes.
  • You have used set, map, priority_queue, deque, and stack each in at least one real problem.
  • You know the complexities of every STL operation you use without looking them up — especially set::lower_bound vs std::lower_bound on a set.
  • You can implement a monotonic stack or monotonic queue from scratch.
  • You have solved at least 5 Div. 2 C problems (or equivalent).

Typical time: 3–6 weeks.

Problems:

Problem Teaches CSES — Traffic Lights set for maintaining positions + multiset for maximum gaps CSES — Room Allocation priority_queue with lazy deletion, sorting + greedy CSES — Nearest Smaller Values Monotonic stack — the canonical template CSES — Sliding Window Median Two heaps (one max-heap, one min-heap) + lazy deletion CSES — Josephus Problem II Order statistics on a dynamic set — needs a Fenwick tree after the set TLEs Codeforces 4C — Registration System map/unordered_map frequency; the operator[] insert-on-read semantics Codeforces 1526B — I Hate 1111 Number theory + the observation that a small case suffices Codeforces 1366A — Shovels and Swords Case analysis + the "when greedy fails" reasoning

docs.title: Phase 4 — Basic Algorithms
docs.text:
The last phase before the "main" CP-Algorithms content (graphs, DP, strings, geometry — covered in later articles of this site).

Mastery criteria:

  • You can solve any problem in CSES "Dynamic Programming" or CSES "Graph Algorithms" that does not require advanced techniques (e.g., no segment trees, no Dijkstra with lazy deletion, no union-find path compression). Basic recursion, memoization, BFS, and DFS suffice.
  • You have implemented BFS and DFS both recursively and iteratively.
  • You have solved at least 10 Div. 2 C and 2 Div. 2 D problems.
  • Your Codeforces rating is at least ~1300 (or you can consistently solve Div. 2 A, B, C).

Typical time: 4–8 weeks.

Problems:

Problem Teaches CSES — Dice Combinations The canonical 1D DP; memoization vs iterative CSES — Minimizing Coins Unbounded knapsack, DP with INF sentinel CSES — Building Roads Connected components via DFS; comparing recursive vs iterative CSES — Message Route BFS on a graph with parent pointers for path reconstruction CSES — Building Teams Bipartite checking via BFS; the coloring pattern CSES — Longest Flight Route Topological sort + DP on DAG (longest path) Codeforces 1611E1 — Escape The Maze (easy) BFS on a tree, multi-source propagation Codeforces 1526C1 — Potions (easy) Greedy with priority queue; contrast with the DP formulation

docs.title: When to move on
docs.text:
Do not move to Phase N+1 until you can honestly check every box in Phase N. The cost of moving early is that Phase N+1 problems are built on Phase N fluency; if you're still looking up lower_bound while solving a DP problem, you'll spend twice as long on each problem and never finish.

The one exception: if you've been stuck on a specific box for two weeks and you're not making progress, move on anyway and come back to it later. Sometimes a perspective from later material clarifies the earlier concept.

docs.title: How to Pick Problems
docs.text: Random problem selection is inefficient. Three systematic approaches:

docs.title: Constraint-based selection
docs.text:
Read the constraints first, reverse-engineer the intended complexity, then pick the technique:

Constraint Likely technique $n \le 20$ Brute force / bitmask DP / permutation enumeration $n \le 100$, $m \le 100$ Floyd–Warshall, $O(n^3)$ DP, small graph algorithms $n \le 2000$ $O(n^2)$ DP or $O(n^2 \log n)$ with care $n \le 10^5$ $O(n \log n)$: sorting, binary search, segment tree, Fenwick, heap $n \le 10^6$ $O(n)$: prefix sums, two pointers, monotonic stack $n \le 10^9$ $O(\log n)$ or $O(\sqrt{n})$: number theory, matrix exponentiation $n \le 10^{18}$ $O(\log n)$: binary lifting, fast exponentiation, digit DP

This table is not a lookup — it's a set of hints. Some $n \le 10^5$ problems are solved by $O(n)$ and some by $O(n \sqrt{n})$. But when you're stuck, "what does the constraint tell me?" is usually enough to break the block.

docs.title: Topic-based selection
docs.text:
Pick a technique, then find 5–10 problems where it's the intended solution. Sources:

  • The "Practice Problems" sections at the bottom of each CP-Algorithms article.
  • CSES Problem Set sections (each is a topic).
  • USACO Guide sections (each has 5–15 practice problems rated by difficulty).

docs.title: Rating-based selection
docs.text:
Pick a rating band ± 200 above your current rating, and solve only problems in that band. Below the band, you're not learning. Above the band, you're stuck and frustrated. The band is where growth happens.

For Codeforces, if your rating is $R$, the band is $[R - 100, R + 200]$. For CSES, the section's "Easy" problems are below the band; the "Hard" problems are above; pick the "Normal" ones.

docs.title: Do not do this
docs.text:
• Don't solve 100 problems at your exact rating. You need the challenge of $R + 200$ to grow.
  • Don't random-select from the full problem archive. This produces a mix of too-easy and too-hard problems, and you don't know which is which until you start.
  • Don't solve 100 problems you already know how to do. If you can look at a problem and immediately write the solution, it's a speed drill (useful occasionally) but not practice.
  • Don't solve problems you don't understand the statement of. If reading the problem twice doesn't tell you what's being asked, the problem is above your reading level, not your coding level.

docs.title: The Upsolve Loop — the Highest-ROI Habit
docs.text: The single activity with the highest return on investment is upsolving: after a contest (or after failing a problem in practice), solve the problems you couldn't solve during the contest. This is where actual skill comes from. The contest is the diagnostic; the upsolve is the treatment.

docs.title: The four-step loop
docs.text:
1. Understand the idea — read the editorial (or someone else's solution) until you can explain the approach to someone else in plain words. Do not look at code yet.
  2. Implement from memory — close the editorial. Open a blank file. Write the solution. If you can't remember the approach, that's the gap; re-read the editorial's idea section, not the code.
  3. Debug and verify — submit. If WA, debug with edge cases. If TLE, think about complexity.
  4. Read the optimal solution — after AC, look at the top 5 submissions on Codeforces for that problem. See if there's a cleaner, shorter, or faster way. Often there is.

The critical step is step 2. Reading an editorial and then copying the code produces zero skill. Closing the editorial and re-deriving the solution is what transfers the idea into your working memory.

docs.title: When to look at the editorial
docs.text:
The "30–60 minutes" rule from most tutorials is too rigid. The right time depends on the problem's difficulty relative to your rating:

Problem rating vs. your rating Time before editorial Below your rating 10 minutes. You should solve these unaided. If you can't, you have a gap in fundamentals that requires targeted practice, not more time on this problem. At your rating 20–30 minutes. This is your learning zone. Struggle is productive, but not for an hour. 100–200 above your rating 45–60 minutes. Some struggle is expected; after an hour, look at a hint (not the full solution), then try for another 15 minutes. 300+ above your rating 10 minutes to read the problem, then skip. These problems are for later. Save the link and come back when you're ready.

The point of the time limit is not to be strict but to avoid grinding on problems you're not equipped to solve. A problem that's 400 points above your rating teaches you nothing because you can't internalize the solution's idea — it's too far from what you know. Save it, get stronger, come back.

docs.title: Stress Testing — the Debugging Method That Actually Works
docs.text: Once you can implement a solution quickly, the bottleneck becomes debugging. The most effective technique is stress testing: generate random small inputs, compare your solution against a brute-force reference, and find the smallest input that produces a mismatch.

docs.title: The four-component model
docs.text:
Every stress test has four files:

  1. gen.cpp — generates a random input (small $n$, random values within the problem's constraints).
  2. brute.cpp — a correct but inefficient solution (usually $O(n^2)$ or $O(2^n)$, fine for $n \le 10$).
  3. sol.cpp — your solution, compiled with -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG -fsanitize=address,undefined.
  4. stress.sh — a shell loop that generates an input, runs both programs, and reports the first mismatch.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# stress.sh — run from a directory containing gen, brute, sol

for i in $(seq 1 1000); do
    ./gen > input.txt
    ./brute < input.txt > out_brute.txt
    ./sol   < input.txt > out_sol.txt

    if ! diff -q out_brute.txt out_sol.txt > /dev/null; then
        echo "Mismatch on iteration $i"
        echo "Input:"
        cat input.txt
        echo "Brute:"
        cat out_brute.txt
        echo "Solution:"
        cat out_sol.txt
        exit 1
    fi

    if [ $((i % 100)) -eq 0 ]; then
        echo "Passed $i iterations"
    fi
done
echo "All 1000 iterations passed"

Compile the three programs with:

g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -o gen   gen.cpp
g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -o brute brute.cpp
g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined -D_GLIBCXX_DEBUG -o sol sol.cpp

The -fsanitize and _GLIBCXX_DEBUG flags make out-of-bounds and undefined behavior fail loudly and immediately, instead of silently producing wrong answers or crashing hours later. They slow the solution by 2–5×, but you're stress testing small inputs anyway, so the slowdown doesn't matter.

docs.title: When stress testing helps
docs.text:
• WA on a test but you don't know why. Almost every time.
  • Suspected edge-case bug. The generator can be designed to produce edge cases (empty, n = 1, all-equal, already-sorted, adversarial patterns).
  • Comparing two algorithms — one you wrote and one you trust.

docs.title: When stress testing doesn't help
docs.text:
• TLE. Stress testing uses small inputs; complexity bugs won't show up. Analyze the algorithm or use the benchmark table from Algorithmic Complexity.
  • Problem statement misunderstanding. If your brute force implements the same wrong interpretation as your solution, both will "agree" and you'll never find the bug. Read the statement again carefully before stress testing.
  • Very large inputs. Generate large test cases separately with a different script; the four-component loop is for small inputs only.

docs.title: Virtual Contests and Contest Strategy
docs.text:
A virtual contest is a replay of a past Codeforces contest under the original 2-hour time limit. You register as if you were participating live, you can see the standings of the original participants, and you get the same feedback loop: which problems were easy (many solves), which were hard (few), and where you should spend your time.

Virtual contests teach three things that regular practice cannot:

  1. Reading a mixed problem set quickly — the ability to skim a problem statement and estimate its difficulty is a skill that transfers directly to real contests.
  2. Time allocation under pressure — you learn what it feels like to be 40 minutes into a contest with 2 WAs and no AC.
  3. The emotional experience of contest day — code that works at home bugs out at 2 PM on Saturday; you learn to stay calm under that specific stress.

docs.title: Contest-day strategy
docs.text:
• First 5 minutes: read all problems A–D. Do not start coding until you know the whole set. The problems are roughly sorted by difficulty, but not always.
  • Next 20–30 minutes: solve A and B. These should be near-instant.
  • Next 30–45 minutes: solve C. This is your learning zone; C is where most people improve.
  • Next 60 minutes: attempt D. If you can't make progress in 20–30 minutes, submit a partial (if the problem allows) or stop and upsolve.
  • Last 10 minutes: re-check your submissions — did you read the output format correctly? Does your solution handle n = 1?

The biggest mistake beginners make is spending the whole contest on C. If C is genuinely beyond you, submitting nothing on D means you lose the chance to upsolve D later with a clear head. Solve fewer, learn more.

docs.title: Speed drills
docs.text: Occasionally (once per week), do a speed drill: take a problem you already know how to solve (e.g., a Div. 2 A from last week), and implement it from scratch in under 10 minutes with zero WA. The goal is not problem-solving; it's coding muscle memory for the STL idioms, the fast I/O template, and the edge-case reflexes. CP is partly a typing contest — if you can't type the solution as fast as you can think it, you lose points on speed alone.

docs.title: Rating Calibration
docs.text:
Codeforces ratings are the lingua franca of competitive programming. Here's what they actually mean:

CF Rating Name Can do Unrated — Solving CSES Introductory problems 800–1000 Newbie Solve Div. 2 A reliably; basic loops and conditionals 1000–1200 Newbie Solve Div. 2 A–B; string manipulation, simple sorting 1200–1400 Pupil Solve Div. 2 B–C; basic prefix sums, two pointers 1400–1600 Specialist Solve Div. 2 C; basic DP, BFS/DFS on trees 1600–1800 Expert Solve Div. 2 D occasionally; segment trees, unions, basic DP on graphs 1800–2000 Expert Solve Div. 2 D reliably; most standard algorithms 2000–2200 Candidate Master Solve Div. 1 B; advanced DP, clever implementations 2200–2400 Master Solve Div. 1 C; full algorithmic toolkit 2400+ Grandmaster Solve Div. 1 D; the top ~1% of competitive programmers

The plateau at 1600–1800 is real and well-documented. Most people who get to Pupil reach Specialist quickly, then get stuck for months or years. The reason is almost always that they are doing the wrong kind of practice: solving more Div. 2 C problems they already can solve, rather than deliberately practicing harder techniques.

Breaking the plateau requires:

  • Moving from "solve problems" to "study techniques" — the D and E problems of Div. 2 require specific algorithms (segment trees with lazy propagation, combinatorial DP on graphs, etc.) that you will not spontaneously invent.
  • Upsolving every D and E from every contest you participate in.
  • Reading other people's solutions and understanding them fully before moving on.
  • Accepting that some problems are simply beyond you for now and moving on without shame.

docs.title: Cross-platform mapping (approximate)
docs.text:
Codeforces AtCoder CSES difficulty 800–1000 ABC A–B Introductory 1200–1400 ABC C–D Sorting and Searching, easy problems 1400–1600 ABC D Sorting and Searching, medium problems 1600–1800 ABC E Data Structures 1800–2000 ABC F Graph Algorithms, Dynamic Programming

The mapping is approximate — AtCoder problems are often conceptually harder than their Codeforces counterparts at the same nominal rating, and CSES problems are often simpler than they look. Use this table as a starting point, not a guarantee.

docs.title: Judges Compared
docs.text:
Judge Best for Problem quality Community When to use CSES Topic-by-topic practice Excellent — clean statements, clear constraints Small (it's a static problem set) Phase 1–4, every phase Codeforces Contests, mixed practice Very good, occasional weak statements Largest and most active Weekly, throughout AtCoder Well-structured contests Excellent, especially for learning Active Weekly (ABC on Saturdays) CodeChef Long contests, consistency Good, sometimes variable Active Optional — useful for sustained practice SPOJ Classical algorithms Variable — many old problems with poor statements Slower, older For specific classical problems USACO Guide Structured learning Very good, curated Small but helpful When you want a "textbook + practice" combination LeetCode Interview prep, not CP Good for interviews, not for CP Large Avoid for CP-specific practice

The single most important judge choice is Codeforces for contests, CSES for topics. Everything else is supplementary.

docs.title: Common Mistakes That Cost Rating
docs.text:
A checklist of the failures you will actually make:

  1. Not reading the problem statement carefully. This is the #1 source of WAs across all levels. Before coding, write down: input format, output format, edge cases, and one worked example by hand. Do not skim.
  2. Ignoring the constraints. $n \le 10^5$ means $O(n \log n)$ is required. If you start coding $O(n^2)$, you will TLE, and you'll have wasted 30 minutes.
  3. Coding before designing. If you open the file before you know what to write, you will code the wrong thing and have to start over. Design on paper first, for 5 minutes.
  4. Not testing on the sample. Always run the sample cases before submitting. Even if you're confident.
  5. Not testing edge cases. n = 1, all-equal input, already-sorted input, negative numbers, empty output. Every one of these has caused a WA for someone.
  6. Skipping upsolve. Solving a problem in a contest is 30% of the learning; upsolving what you missed is the other 70%.
  7. Looking at the editorial too early. Reading an editorial after 10 minutes trains you to expect the answer to appear. Reading it after 45 minutes trains you to actually think.
  8. Looking at the editorial too late. Grinding on a problem 400 points above your rating for 2 hours is not "productive struggle"; it's wasted time.
  9. Not reading other people's code. After AC, look at the top 5 submissions. There's always something to learn.
  10. Ignoring the "purple problem" phenomenon. Some problems at 1800–2000 have weird, unimplementable solutions. Skip them; not every problem teaches you something useful.
  11. Skipping implementations. Reading a solution and understanding it is not the same as implementing it. You need the typing practice.
  12. Practicing only one technique. Doing 100 prefix-sum problems doesn't make you a better competitive programmer; it makes you a prefix-sum specialist. Rotate topics.
  13. Practicing only contests. Contests don't teach new techniques; they only test existing ones. If you never read a new technique, you'll never learn one.
  14. Comparing to others too much. Rating is relative. Your progress is absolute. Track your own problem-solving rate over time.
  15. Not sleeping before contests. A tired brain loses 200–300 rating points. Real.
  16. Assuming TLE means "code too slow". TLE can also mean "wrong algorithm" (an $O(n^2)$ where $O(n)$ is needed) or "wrong I/O" (cin without sync_with_stdio(false) on 10^6 inputs). Diagnose before optimizing.
  17. Submitting without compiling locally. A trivial error — a missing ;, a typo in a variable name — will get rejected. Compile, run the sample, then submit.
  18. Not learning from failure. If you look at the editorial and then close it, you learned nothing. If you read it, understand it, close it, re-implement it, then submit — you learned it.
  19. Overfitting to your own bugs. If a solution WAs on test 5, don't just patch test 5. Understand what test 5 represents; the bug affects other inputs too.
  20. Forgetting the -O2 flag locally. Your code TLEs on the judge but runs in 1 second on your machine. Compile with -O2 locally to match the judge.

docs.title: Recommended Learning Path
docs.text:
A realistic timeline, calibrated for someone who has ~1–2 hours per day:

Month Focus 1 Finish the C++ course, complete CSES "Introductory Problems" 2 CSES "Sorting and Searching", start Div. 3 virtual contests 3–4 CSES "Data Structures", weekly Div. 2 and Div. 3 virtuals 5–6 CSES "Dynamic Programming" and "Graph Algorithms", start real contests 7–12 Start the "main" CP-Algorithms content (graphs, trees, strings, geometry), participate in every contest you can

The "main" CP-Algorithms content in this course is covered in later articles; this article focused on the prerequisite path. Once you have solid Phase 4 mastery, the graph algorithms, dynamic programming, strings, and geometry sections are within reach.

The single most important habit to build in the first year is upsolving. It will feel like a chore. It is the only thing that works.

  • USACO Guide — the best-structured roadmap for competitive programming. Every topic has a difficulty rating, curated problems, and short explanations.
